Location: County: Mantanuska - Susnita Borough                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Location: Additional Location Information: The Property is located 60 kilometers (km) northwest from Haines, Alaska, in the Alaska panhandle.
The Property lies 2 km from the Haines Highway, which links the deep-sea port of Haines, Alaska. The Palmer project would sit in the watershed of the Chilkat River,  The Palmer Project is a copper, zinc, gold, silver and barite deposit that sits above Glacier Creek, about 35 miles north of Haines. Glacier Creek is a tributary to the Klehini and Chilkat rivers. The Tlingit village of Klukwan sits about 15 miles downstream from the mine at the confluence of the Chilkat and Klehini rivers.                                                                             Project Description: Change in Ownership: In a deal announced in 2024,  Dowa Metals and Mining, a Japanese company, will give up its roughly 70% interest in the Palmer Project near the Southeast Alaska communities of Haines and Klukwan. Taking over is American Pacific Mining Corp., a Canadian company that owns no operating mines and instead focuses on exploring deposits that could become mines later on. It’s set to take full ownership of the project by the end of the year, up from its current 30% minority stake

Project Name: Name of Project was changed from Clayton Valley Project to Angel Island Mine to distinguish from other Clayton Valley developments.
Location: Additional Location Information:  Located in west-central Nevada (219 miles southeast of Reno and 206 miles northwest of Las Vegas), immediately east of Albemarle’s active Silver Peak lithium mine. The town of Silver Peak is 6 miles west, Goldfield is 24 miles east, Tonopah is 41 miles northeast.
Project Description: Mining Method: Will extract lithium from sedimentary clay, similar to Thacker Pass and Rhyolite Ridge; will use hydrochloric acid instead of sulphuric acid as the solvent.
Project Description: Status of Project:  Since the completion of a Feasibility Study of Angel Island in April 2024, the developer’s attention has been on process optimization to drive reductions in the Project’s estimated capital and operating costs, environmental studies and permitting, and Project funding. 
Project Description: Regulatory Challenges: Conflict over water rights in the water-stressed area.  
Developer Description: Lead Developer: Name of developer was changed from Cypress Development Corporation to Century Lithium Corporation in 2023.
Commercial Plans: Processing Done by the Same Lead Developer/Parent Company:  Yes, at a facility 125 miles south.  Metallurgical testing on Project material indicates low-cost processing can be achieved with conventional tank leaching and counter current decantation, resulting in low acid consumption and high lithium recovery of over 85% of total lithium. Lithium extraction facility at del Sol Refining in Amargosa Valley, Nevada. The operation of the Pilot Plant is providing essential data for the ongoing Feasibility Study; Employs a hydrochloric acid leaching process combined with Onyx's 2021-acquired ion exchange DLP technology and Saltworks Technologies' refining process to produce high-purity 99.94% LCE, exceeding battery-grade standards.
Land Ownership: Type of Land: 5,845 acres of BLM.

Location: County: Northwest Arctic Borough of Alaska
Location: Additional Location Information:  Southern Brooks Range of arctic region of Alaska approximately 168 miles east of Kotzebue, 22 miles northeast of Kobuk, 162 miles west of the Dalton Highway; 292 miles northwest of Fairbanks. 
Project Description: Mining Method: An open pit mine that will include infrastructure such as a tailings management facility, a waste rock facility, a tailings dam, a waste rock collection pond, multiple water treatment plants, a mill facility, a crusher facility, an ore stockpile building, and a concentrate  facility. 
Project Description: Existing Mine: No previous mining but exploratory drilling at the Arctic deposit and within the Ambler Mining District has been ongoing since its discovery in 1966. Approximately 67,639 meters of drilling was completed within the Ambler Mining District, including 55,038 meters of drilling in 285 drill holes at the Arctic deposit or on potential extensions. Drill programs were completed by Kennecott and its subsidiaries, Anaconda, NovaGold, Trilogy and Ambler Metals. 
Project Description: Status of Project: The public debate has focused on the proposed Ambler Road that is designed to connect the mine to the Dalton Highway. The mining project itself may also be controversial. The 211-mile-long Ambler Road was initially approved under the Trump administration, which issued, through the Army Corps of Engineers and BLM, a 50-year right-of-way permit to build the road just before President Donald Trump left office.  Under the Biden administration, the federal government revised the Trump-era environmental impact assessment, found unacceptable environmental risks, and disallowed the permit. The decision against proceeding with the project was contained in a final supplemental environmental impact statement released by BLM.
Developer Description: Parent Company: Joint Venture of South 32 Limited (AU) and Trilogy Metals Inc. (CA). NovaGold Resources Inc. acquired the Arctic Project from Kennecott in 2004. In 2011, NovaGold transferred all copper projects to NovaCopper Inc. and in 2012 spun-out NovaCopper to its then existing shareholders. NovaCopper Inc. subsequently underwent a name change to Trilogy Metals Inc. in 2016. The Project is directly held by Ambler Metals LLC in a 50/50 joint venture between South32 and Trilogy Metals (February 2020). Upon the formation of the joint venture, Trilogy Metals contributed all of its Alaskan assets, including the Project , to Ambler Metals in exchange for a 50% membership interest; at the same time, South32 contributed $145 million in cash for a 50% membership interest.
Commerical Plans: Planned Production Capacity: The developer announced the results of an updated Arctic Feasibility Study (FS) on February 14, 2023.  
Commercial Plans: Processing Done by the Same Lead Developer/Parent Company: The conclusions of test work conducted both in 2012 and 2017 indicate that the Arctic materials are well-suited to the production of high-quality copper and zinc concentrates using flotation techniques, which are industry standard.  The process plant will produce three concentrates: copper concentrate, zinc concentrate, and lead concentrate. 
Land Ownership: Type of Land: The project area consists of 18 federal patented mining claims, which cover an area of approximately 272 acres and 1,341 state mineral claims that cover an area of approximately 114,000 acres. In total, the Project area comprises approximately 114,498 acres of state and federal (BLM) mining claims. 
Statements of Support from Public Officials: State: In a December 2023 letter, the Alaska congressional delegation, led by senior US Senator Lisa Murkowski, criticized the Biden administration for delaying the Ambler Road environmental analysis and urged it to advance the project; GOP Gov. Mike Dunleavy of Alaska also advocates for the development of the Ambler Road.
Statements of Support from Public Officials: Federal: Rep. Mary Peltola, a Democrat and Alaska’s only member of the House of Representatives, did not entirely oppose the Biden administration’s decision but called for new dialogue that would find an acceptable path forward for the private road.  
Statements of Concern from Public Officials: Federal:  In a 2024 effort to force the BLM to approve the Ambler Road, it was included in an initial draft of a must-pass defense appropriations bill.  Senate Democrats removed the provision due to strong concerns registered by opponents of the road.
Litigation: Evidence of Litigation: The Tanana Chiefs Conference, which represents 42 villages in interior Alaska, many of which are located near to the proposed Ambler Road, sued the Interior Department in 2020 over its handling of the environmental analysis, arguing that it did not adequately address impacts to their way of life.  This lawsuit was not resolved when the Biden administration took office, and the lawsuit was set aside while the administration revisited the environmental impact statement.
Concerned Interest Groups: Indigenous Groups: A majority of Tribes in Alaska including the United Tribes of Bristol Bay
Concerned Interest Groups: Scale of Environmental Groups: Local -- Audubon Society Alaska;  National -- Center for Biological Diversity
Concerned Interest Groups: Recreational Groups: Backcountry Hunters and Anglers (BHA).  BHA is part of a coalition of conservation organizations, Alaska-based outfitters, and national hunting and fishing companies that have publicly opposed the Ambler Road since the fall of 2023. That group, known as Hunters & Anglers for the Brooks Range, also lists Trout Unlimited and the National Deer Association as coalition partners. Arctic Fishing Adventures in Kotzebue, Alaska, who guides out-of-state anglers looking to catch tarpon-like sheefish through the ice in the Brooks Range, also opposed the Road.
Reasons for Concern: Impacts to Natural Environment: The Ambler Road would cross 26 miles of Gates of the Arctic National Park and Preserve. 
Reasons for Concern: Traffic & Noise: As many as 168 truck trips per day
Reasons for Concern: Water Quality: The Ambler Road would cross hundreds of rivers and streams and could lead to pollution of some Alaska’s most important salmon and sheefish spawning streams
Reasons for Concern: Subsistence Hunting/Fishing: More than 30 tribal communities might face restrictions on subsistence hunting and fishing if the Ambler Road were built — a key factor in the Biden administration’s reasoning; The Road could also hurt caribou migration patterns even though hunting caribou is central to the subsistence lifestyle of nearby native Alaskan villagers
Supportive Interest Groups: Commercial Groups: The Alaska Native corporation in the region, known as NANA Corp, also owns some of the subsurface rights in the mining district and has a longstanding partnership with Ambler Metals to develop the deposit. It once supported the Ambler Road. But it withdrew its support in March 2024.  NANA is owned by the Iñupiat people of Northwest Alaska. Without support from NANA, the state will need to bend the road to the north to avoid some land owned by NANA.  
Reasons for Support: Economic Growth: The Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority Board, the state’s development bank, initially filed for federal permits to build the Ambler Road in 2015 and approved about $44.8 million toward the project. It argued the mining district is estimated to create more than 3,900 direct and indirect jobs, and more than $300 million in annual wages, adding new revenues to state and local coffers.
Reasons for Support: Community Development: The populations of nearby villages are 151 in Kobuk (2020 Census), 210 in Shungnak (2020 Census), and 275 in Ambler (2020 Census). Residents largely live a subsistence lifestyle with incomes supplemented by tour guiding, local development projects, employment through tribal and city councils, government aid, and employment both in and outside of their home villages. The Arctic Project has the potential to significantly improve work opportunities for residents during the exploration phase, construction, and during full operation. The Tanana Chiefs Conference, which represents 42 villages in interior Alaska, many of which are near the proposed Ambler Road, sued the Interior Department in 2020 over its handling of the environmental analysis, arguing that it did not adequately address impacts to their way of life. After the lawsuit was filed, though, three of the villages switched sides and said they support the Road because of its economic benefits to the villages and the State.

Location: Additional Location Information:  Located just west of the company town of Bagdad (pop 2,661, 2022), 100 miles northwest of Phoenix, Arizona, within the Upper Burro Creek Wilderness area.
Project Description: Status of Project: Mining on site since 1906; The Bagdad copper mine in Arizona (active) is in a feasibility analysis of a plan to double its concentrator capacity, but the urgency of the plan has been removed due to somewhat low copper prices.  The capital costs of the expansion cannot be justified at the current copper prices but higher copper prices would allow the expansion to move forward; The Bagdad mine is expected to be the first with a fully autonomous haulage system as a part of the process of converting its existing manned fleet to 100% autonomous operation.
Developer Description: Was There Change in Ownership during Project?:Purchased from Boston Consolidated Mining Company in 1989. 
Commercial Plans: Planned Production Capacity: currently 25% of US demand.

Project Name: The BamaStar Project site was previously home to a mine known as the Ceylon Graphite Project, which operated during World War I and World War II.
Location: Additional Location Information:  East-central Alabama near Alexander City (pop 14,843, 2020), at the northeast end of the 60-mile Alabama Graphite Belt.  Located 8 miles northeast of Sylacauga (pop 12,578, 2020), 48 miles from Birmingham, and about 225 miles northeast of the major Gulf-of-Mexico port of Mobile, Alabama. 
Project Description: Status of Project: Plan to be operational by 2027; In November 2024, the developer filed positive results and favorable economics in its Preliminary Economic Assessment; the assessment includes a graphite mine, a concentrate processing facility and a value-add plant for upgrading and transforming the graphite concentrates precursor. 
Developer Description: Was There Change in Ownership during Project?:  Westwater is focused on battery-grade natural graphite after its acquisition of Alabama Graphite Corp. (AGC) in April 2018. AGC acquired the Project in 2012 based on the geological setting. On April 23, 2018, Westwater acquired a 100% interest in AGC as part of a strategic decision to refocus the Company to supply battery manufacturers with low-cost, high-quality, and high-margin natural graphite products.
Commercial Plans: Planned Production Capacity: The Coosa graphite concentrator facilities are designed to process 90,000 tonnes per year of flotation concentrate product grading 95% Cg.
Financial Support: Federal Agency: DOD: $3.2 million for feasibility study                                                                                                                                                                                               
Statements of Support from Public Officials: State: Governor of Alabama supports.
Statements of Support from Public Officials: Federal: Biden Administration.

Location: Additional Location Information: Located in west-central Arizona, around 6 miles from the operating Bagdad copper mine.
Project Description: Status of Project: Exploration began in 2018, drilling continues in 2024, east and west basin areas. 8,800 feet of core drilling is planned. Next steps include continuing the environmental assessment process (leading to a PEA), and drilling 52 boreholes.

Location: Additional Location Information:  2 miles northwest of Sundance, northeast Wyoming, off I-90 in the Northern Black Hills, an isolated mountain range extending from western South Dakota into Wyoming.
Project Description: Status of Project: Development. The developer’s goal is to begin mine production in 2029.
Project Description: Regulatory Challenges: In January 2016 the developer, after almost a decade of work, suspended the NEPA process for the overall project at USFS in the face of concerted opposition from tribal and environmental groups. The developer will need to restart and complete this process to obtain a federal permit for mining. In November 2023 DOE completed the NEPA process to support its financial assistance of the separation and processing demonstration plant.
Commercial Plans: Processing Plan in US: The developer has a well-developed processing plan at a facility in the nearby town of Upton, Wyoming. A pilot demonstration plant for the new separation and treatment technology will begin in 2025. The plant is partially subsidized by the US Department of Energy.
Financial Support: Federal Agency: In 2024, the grant amount increased from 20 million to 24.2 million, specifically for the processing plant.
Land Ownership: Type of Land: The project site is located on a mix of federal (USFS), state and private land; a total of approximately 8,000 acres.
Reasons for Concern: Site of Historical, Cultural, Spiritual Significance: Concern over impacts to tribal culture

Location: Additional Location Information: Northern Arizona on Interstate 93 (I-93) near small town of Wikieup, about halfway between Phoenix and Las Vegas.
Project Description: Status of Project: The developer experienced a setback in August 2024 when a federal judge ordered an injunction against exploratory drilling while the judge rules on the merits of a lawsuit by the Hualapai Tribe and the nonprofit environmental law organization Earthjustice.  The lawsuit challenged BLM's approval of the exploratory drilling, arguing that the project threatens Ha'Kamwe', a medicinal spring recognized as a traditional cultural property. It also asserted that drilling could impact aquifers, wildlife, and other vital resources in the area.
Project Description: Regulatory Challenges: Unpatented mining claims on the site of the project led to a dispute with another developer that took two years to be fully resolved; the developer was delayed in obtaining a third exploratory permit from BLM due to intense opposition from nearby tribes and others.   The request for the third exploratory program was filed on March 12, 2021.  The public comment period began in April 2021 and was extended twice.  The developer ultimately agreed to several changes to the exploration plan to secure BLM approval in June 2024. The first and second exploratory activities were in 2019, 16 holes covering 1.57 acres and then 37 holes covering 4.98 acres.  The third permit allows 131 holes covering 21 acres over an 18-month period. In late 2024, a federal court issued an injunction against BLM’s approval of exploration (third phase) on the grounds of inadequate consultation with tribal groups and threat to a historical and spiritual site.
Developer Description: Lead Developer: partnered with Navajo Transitional Energy Company- handling operations and permitting process
Commercial Plans: Processing Plan in US: Preliminary tests with contractors Hazen Research & KCA to determine feasibility. Using sulphuric acid to extract Li
Litigation: Evidence of Litigation: In August of 2024, a federal judge overturned the third exploratory drilling plan that was approved by the BLM earlier in June, even though plan was changed extensively to accommodate some tribal concerns. Litigants included EarthJustice and a local tribe. In November of 2024, the US District Court For the District of Arizona ordered that Arizona Lithium cannot continue any work that was previously authorized by BLM’s June 6th or 9th decision letters. The Hualapai Tribe’s request to extend the temporary restraining order into a preliminary injunction was also granted.
Concerned Interest Groups: Indigenous Groups: Nearby Native American Tribe- Hualapai Tribe.
Concerned Interest Groups: Scale of Environmental Groups: National -- Earthjustice; Regional -- Great Basin Resource Watch.
Concerned Interest Groups: Commercial Groups: Concerned farmers and ranchers.
Reasons for Concern: Site of Historical, Cultural, Spiritual Significance:
The Hualapai Tribe expressed concerns of noise, vibrations and potential damage done to soil and plants. The development is near the Tribe's sacred hot spring. The Tribe has expressed concerns for the their local water sources and potential damage to the hot spring with the risk of puncturing aquifers. The concern for their land and hot spring had led to protests.
Reasons for Concern: Inadequate Community Engagement: Poor consultation with tribes. 
Supportive Interest Groups: Commercial Groups: Navajo Transitional Company

Location: Additional Location Information: Located near town of Herriman (55,144, 2020), Salt Lake County, Utah. Eastern portion of the Oquirrh Mountains, approximately 16 miles south-west of the Salt Lake City, Utah, US.
Project Description: Existing Mine: One of the largest open-pit copper mines in the world; it began operations in 1906. Since acquiring the Kennecott operations in 1989, Rio Tinto has invested more than $5 billion towards modernisation, environmental upgrades and mine-life extension.
Project Description: Status of Project: Rio Tinto is expanding the underground portion of the mine with a $920 million investment. Copper production from the underground north rim skarn began in 2024; operations are planned to deliver around 250,000 tons of mined copper over the next 10 years, roughly 25% of US copper consumption.
Developer Description: Lead Developer: The company was first formed in 1898 as the Boston Consolidated Mining Company. The current corporation was formed in 1989.
Developer Description: Was There Change in Ownership during Project?: Rio Tinto acquired the Kennecott operations in 1989.
Commercial Plans: Processing Done by the Same Lead Developer/Parent Company: Virtually all processing is performed on site. Crushed ore is transported on a 5-mile conveyor and stockpiled at the Concentrator, where it is ground into fine particles. After treatment with air, water, and chemical reagents, the concentrate is transported to a smelter via pipeline.
Statements of Support from Public Officials: State: Both Utah Governor Spencer Cox and Lt. Governor Deidre Henderson have made public appearances at the site, touting the developer's modernization programs, including the transition to all-electric trucks.
Concerned Interest Groups: Community Residents/Groups: Save Our Canyons.
Reasons for Concern: Air Quality: Underground mines tend to be a significant source of dust emissions while the developer's nearby copper smelter is a significant source of air emissions in the county. Air quality improved after the developer installed better scrubbers on the smelter smokestack.
Reasons for Concern: Water Quality: The developer is well into more than a dozen expensive moving and construction projects to clean up and contain its hazardous wastes, and it is working on plans to deal with major long-term problems, such as groundwater contamination. Some activists fear that the shift to more underground operations could dry up or pollute nearby aquifers. 
Reasons for Support: Cleaner than Other Sources: The developer is switching from coal to renewable energy. Kennecott Utah Copper owned and operated a coal-fired power plant in Magna that earlier supplied electricity for the mine and processing operations. The power station was shut down in 2017 after being operated for 75 years. In May 2019, Rio Tinto announced that the operations will receive power through 1.5 million megawatt hours (MWh) of renewable energy certificates purchased from Rocky Mountain Power. It is expected to reduce the carbon footprint of the Kennecott operation by approximately 65%.

Location: Additional Location Information: Located 17 miles north of White Sulphur Springs (955, 2020), central Montana.
Project Description: Status of Project: Development. Mine construction was delayed during years of litigation over the Montana DEQ operating permit.  The developer has not yet announced a timetable for construction after the favorable 2024 decision of the Montana State Supreme Court.
Project Description: Regulatory Challenges: The developer is managing opposition from several conservation groups and mayors of towns that are downstream of the planned project. In 2018 the developer helped defeat (56% - 44%) a statewide ballot proposition (Montana I-186) that would have restricted permitting for mining projects such as Black Butte. The developer is also managing two sets of multi-year lawsuits against its permits, and both cases reached the Montana Supreme Court.
Statements of Support from Public Officials: Local: Local support for the project is strong. The Meagher County commission gave its approval to Sandfire’s mine impact plan. Many businesses along the town’s Main St. display weathered signs in their front windows proclaiming support for the project..
Litigation: Evidence of Litigation: In 2024 the Montana Supreme Court upheld the project's operating permit, reversing the lower court's decision. A separate lawsuit alleged the Montana Department of Environmental Quality should have required more permits for the project's planned usage of groundwater. The Montana Supreme Court heard the case in March 2024 and has not yet released a decision.
Concerned Interest Groups: Environmental Groups: Save Our Smith coalition formed in opposition to the mine. Montana Trout Unlimited also opposes the mine.
Reasons for Concern: Water Quality: The Smith River is 20 miles downstream of the project site, with Sheep Creek (near the project site) flowing into it.
Reasons for Concern: Recreation: Popular boating areas (Smith River) are nearby.

Location: Additional Location Information: Near Cobalt (pop 13, 2020), central Idaho. 
Project Description: Existing Mine: Land includes old Blackpine copper mine operated from 1945 to 1965.
Project Description: Status of Project: In FY 2023 Annual Report the developer stated there was no significant exploration activity at the site and no progress has been made; Koba Resources reports in its FY 2024 Annual Report that no significant work was done at its cobalt projects in FY 2024.
Land Ownership: Type of Land: Public land with US Forest Service oversight.

Location: Additional Location Information: Near town of Silver Peak (pop 121, 2020), Clayton Valley, Esmeralda County, Nevada. Directly adjoins the western portion of lithium producer Albemarle’s evaporation ponds and is nearby Century Lithium Corp.’s proposed 5,430-acre Angel Island Lithium Mine.                                                                                        Status of Project:  In 2022 the developer’s maiden drill program revealed a new lithium discovery through Blue Clay Lithium Project in Clayton Valley. Lithium values as high as 1230 ppm Li were encountered with 800 ppm Li over 120 feet, including 1,011 ppm Li over 40 feet.                                                                                                                                          Change in Ownership: The developer closed an option agreement dated September 30, 2021 to acquire the Blue Clay Lithium Project in Clayton Valley Nevada. This project consists of 94 contiguous claims totaling approximately 1950 acres prospective for lithium.

Location: Additional Location Information: Near Cobalt (pop 13, 2020), central Idaho.
Project Description: Status of Project:  In the first quarter of 2024, the developer reported no field activity at the site.  
Land Ownership: Type of Land: 3,200 hectare Bonanza Project holdings.

Location: Additional Location Information: Nearest town is Beatty (population 880, 2020), 25 miles southeast; Beatty is 8 miles east of Death Valley National Park in southeast Nevada; 125 miles northwest of Las Vegas, Nevada.
Project Description: Mining Method: Borehole extraction method.
Project Description: Existing Mine: Previous industrial site – milling for local mines in the 1900s.
Project Description: Status of Project: The 2024 drilling program extended to 2,807 feet and intersected the northeast continuation of the high-grade Lithium and Boron mineralized zone. The 518 ft intercept is the thickest +5,000 ppm lithium interval drilled to date.
Developer Description: Was There Change in Ownership during Project?:  Iconic Minerals LTD first staked the land, then split ownership 50/50 with Nevada Lithium Resources Inc. before Nevada Lithium Inc. secured 100% ownership of the project.  
Commercial Plans: Processing Plan in US: Mineral processing has been planned to be conducted on-site, however this is still in the development phase; 
Land Ownership: Type of Land: Private Land - 18300-acre land package.

Location: Additional Location Information: Near town of Fields (pop 120, 2010), in Alvord Desert, southeast Oregon. 
Project Description: Status of Project: Work at the site ended in 2022 when the BLM determined that the claims were in an area of eastern Oregon that Congress withdrew from mining in a federal conservation law called the Steens Act of 2,000.  
Project Description: Regulatory Challenges: The land this project was planned for is off-limits to mining per an action by Congress.
Concerned Interest Groups: Scale of Environmental Groups: Regional -- Regional Wildlands Defense

Location: Additional Location Information:  Located on western edge of Mojave Desert, near town of Boron (pop 2,086, 2020), south-central California. Boron was a mining town established soon after a borax deposit was discovered in 1925. Site of California’s largest open-pit mine (boron) and largest boronate mine in the world.
Project Description: Status of Project: Development of the lithium project at Boron draws on developer’s long standing partnership with the U.S. Department of Energy’s Critical Materials Institute (CMI), which is committed to discovering ways to economically recover critical mineral by-products from existing refining and smelting processes. CMI experts worked alongside the developer’s technical leads to help solve a number of key processing challenges to produce battery grade lithium at Boron. The next step is to scale up the project.
Financial Support: Federal Agency: In-kind assistance through technical collaboration with DOE’s Critical Materials Institute; no grant or loan.

Location: Additional Location Information: Outside Sheridan (pop 18,737), in north central Wyoming                                                                                             Project Descriptions: Regulatory Challenges: The developer originally thought it could initiate rare earth mining under its 2020 coal mining permit.  However, it may be necessary to obtain a separate permit for rare-earth mining insofar as the method is different in environmental impacts could be somewhat different.  Nicole Pollack. Questions Remain for Rare Earths Mining Project in Northern Wyoming. Star Tribune, May 22, 2023; updated June 24, 2024.                                                                                                                               Developer Description: Lead Developer: Ramaco Resources (US, coal producer).  Even Ramaco itself is a relative newcomer; the miner with properties in West Virginia and Virginia was founded in 2011, went public in 2017 and has since grown to a run rate of 5 million tons annually (with plans to expand to 7+ Mtpy as the market allows), over 1,000 employees and reserves of roughly 60 million tons.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Developer Description: Was There Change in Ownernship during Project?: Ramaco purchased the Brook mine in 2011. It had been continuously owned by Pittston Coal since 1912                                        Land Ownership: Type of Land: Private -- The Brook Mine comprises over 15,800 acres outside of Sheridan, Wyoming, one of the largest privately controlled mineral reserves in the Western United States. Roughly 4,500 acres were permitted for mining in 2020, which is where the initial assessment program has been conducted. Mining at the Brook Mine could begin as early as the fourth quarter of 2023, following additional mining development and assessment. The additional 11,300 acres will be also assessed and could provide opportunity to increase the scale of the overall development in the future.                                                                                                                                                                             Statements of Support from Public Officials: Representative Cyrus Western (R-Big Horn)                                                                                                                                                           Concerned Intersest Groups: Community Residents/Groups: Powder River Basin Council (landowners group that has been battling coal development for years).  The Council influenced the developer’s July 2020 coal mining permit, which has conditions addressing land subsidence as well as sage grouse protection.                                              Reasons for Concern: Water Quality: The developer started by looking at mining of coal but has shifted to rare earths.  The Powder River Basin Resource Council is concerned. It has been fighting Ramaco for years, back when the company still planned to mine coal. Residents worried how its presence might affect air and water quality, according to Wyoming Public Radio. With plans for the mine shifting to REEs, the PRBRC seems to still have concerns, according to The Casper Star-Tribune.

Location: Additional Location Information:  Located 43 miles south of Phoenix International Airport and 6.2 miles south of the city of Casa Grande (pop 55,653, 2020), Arizona.  
Project Description: Mining Method: 94% of mined material from open pit (Cactus West and Parks/Salyer), 6% from the Stockpile and Cactus East underground.
Project Description: Existing Mine: Yes. ASARCO operated copper mine from 1974-1984.   It was called the Sacaton mine.  
Project Description: Status of Project:  The developer completed a Preliminary Economic Assessment in the third quarter of 2024 following an updated mineral resource estimate from July 2024.  The next step is a definitive feasibility study.   
Developer Description: Lead Developer: Arizona Sonoran Copper (ASCU) has granted Nuton (a subsidiary of Rio Tinto Inc) an exclusive right and option to acquire between a 35% and 40% interest in its Cactus project.
Developer Description: Was There Change in Ownership during Project?: Developer acquired project from ASARCO Trust in July 2020.  
Commercial Plans: Processing Done by the Same Lead Developer/Parent Company:Copper cathodes will be produced directly onsite through heap leaching, solvent extraction, and electrowinning (SXEW), including a four-year ramp-up period.

Location: Additional Location Information: Located about 30 miles west of Charlotte, North Carolina, near the town of Cherryville (pop 6,707, 2020) within the Carolina Tin-Spodumene Belt.  From the 1950s to the 1980s, the Carolina Tin-Spodumene Belt provided nearly all the world’s lithium, delivering important supply chain resources to the U.S. military as well as the automotive, glass, ceramics, and pharmaceutical industries.
Project Description: Mining Method: Plan for 4 new open pit mines, each 50 feet deep, 1,500 acres.
Project Description: Existing Mine: Site is location of old lithium mines that closed in 1980s and 1990s (competition from South America)
Project Description: Status of Project: The developer no longer has an explicit schedule for starting production but in 2024 secured a critical state permit
Project Description: Regulatory Challenges: It took the developer several years longer than expected to obtain necessary state permits.  The required rezoning by the Gaston County Commissioners has not yet occurred.
Developer Description: Parent Company: The Australian company Sayona is buying Piedmont Lithium (developer of Carolina Lithium in Gaston County).  CEO of Piedmont Lithium is turning over and Sanona will become parent of a new subsidiary that includes Piedmont Lithium.
Commercial Plans: Processing Done by the Same Lead Developer/Parent Company: The developer replaced a planned processing plant at the mine site with a new plant in Tennessee ($141.7 million federal grant) with mined ore from Quebec and Ghana util Carolina Lithium is operational; however, in 2024 the developer, facing financial challenges, decided not to proceed with the processing plant in Tennessee.
Financial Support: Public Supply Agreement w/ an Automaker or Battery/Component Producer: The developer in 2020 signed a deal to supply Tesla from Carolina Lithium. Tesla agreed to buy 160,000 tons/year of spodumene for at least five years (the expectation was it would come from the new Gaston County mine); first deliveries were scheduled for July 2022 and July 2023; The Tesla deal was amended in January 2023 to 125,000 tons per year from 2023-2025 (the likely source being Piedmont Lithium’s lithium mine in Quebec, Canada in partnership with Sayona Quebec)
Land Ownership: Type of Land: Company controls 3,100 acres of private land. 
Statements of Support from Public Officials: Local: Mayor and town officials of Cherryville (nearest town) are cooperating with the developer.
Statements of Support from Public Officials: Federal: Support from US Senator Thom Tillis (R-NC)
Statements of Concern from Public Officials: Local: Gaston County Commission (which must rezone site to allow mining) imposed a 60-day moratorium on development while it revised local zoning laws to limit blasting and truck traffic; local officials were irked that the developer's CEO did not attend an informational meeting with the Gaston County Board of Commissioners; The chair of the Commission and other members expressed skepticism/opposition toward the project. The mine likely cannot proceed without a rezoning action by the Gaston County Commissioners; if the County declines to rezone, the developer could go to court and seek a reversal of the County’s decision. Several seats on the Commission turned over in the November 2024 election.
Litigation: Evidence of Litigation: On January 18, 2024, the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of New York granted the developer's motion to dismiss a securities class action lawsuit, originally filed in July 2021, against Piedmont and two of its executives.  Additional shareholder lawsuits are unresolved, where the allegation is that the developer misrepresented the prospects for mining at the site.
Concerned Interest Groups: Community Residents/Groups: Some local homeowners sold their land to the developer as early as 2017 but some refused, and formed the local opposition group STOP PIEDMONT LITHIUM; 100+ residents attended a public town hall -- the public felt upset with the rollout of the mine's development plan as they perceived they were last to be approached after all other stakeholders.  
Reasons for Concern: Water Supply: Local residents are concerned that the 500-foot mine could cause water wells in the area to dry up.  The developer offered to help residents dig deeper wells or connect to municipal water supplies.
Reasons for Concern: Water Quality: Possible arsenic pollution by releasing naturally-occurring arsenic into surface and groundwater. 
Reasons for Concern: Reputation of the Developer/Parent Company: The developer upset the local community by not involving the community in the creation of the plan. 
Reasons for Concern: Other: Home damage from blasting.

Location: Additional Location Information: Located 20 miles west of Cheyenne (65,132, 2020), near Curt Gowdy State Park, southeastern Wyoming. 
Project Description: Mining Method: Open pit, using froth flotation to extract the materials; 80 acres, 800 feet deep.
Project Description: Existing Mine: Copper King Mine started in 1881, was an underground operation, and Herc ceased operation just prior to World War II.  Much exploratory drilling by several developers since then.  In 2016 US Gold Corporation acquired 100% of the mineral leases.  
Project Description: Status of Project: The State granted US Gold an operating permit in April/May 2024; a reclamation bond was put up for any initial disturbance in May 2024; water discharge permit was granted in June 2024; and the last required permit, the air permit, was granted in November 2024. Now the developer will prepare a  feasibility study and raise capital for construction; Prefeasibility study released December 2021, to be updated summer of 2024. Industrial siting permit approved June 20, 2023. General permit application submitted to Wyoming Department of Environmental Quality in 2022; permit awarded April 29, 2024. Water permit awarded June 2024.  Working on air permit. 
Developer Description: Lead Developer: Subsidiary Gold King Corporation.
Processing: Some onsite processing but more advanced processing at existing offsite locations in US and/or abroad. 
Land Ownership: Public Land Ownership: A large portion of the mine will be on state-owned lands known as school trust lands, which means the royalties generated from it will go toward the state's school system. 
Reasons for Concern: Recreation: Close proximity to Curt Gowdy State Park.

Location: Additional Location Information: Located near Silver Peak (pop 213, 2022), 5 miles from Goldfield (pop 268, 2010), county seat of Esmeralda County, 30 miles west-southwest of Tonopah (pop 2,478, 2010), northwest quadrant of Clayton Valley, Nevada; less than 200 miles from Las Vegas; adjacent to Albemarle’s active Silver Peak lithium mine and the claims/exploration by Pure Energy Minerals.
Project Description: Status of Project: In March 2024, the developer filed a NI 43-101 technical report with an estimated inferred lithium carbon equivalent (LCE) resource of 302,900 metric tons over a 40-year extraction period. 
Project Description: Regulatory Challenges: The current state ground water regulation is the most serious issue for the Project. Clayton Valley is now judged to be over allocated and new diversions are not granted. To move into production, ACME will need to get permitting and allocation for water rights from the State of Nevada, purchase water rights from an existing holder, or see changes in how brines are regulated similar to geothermal fluids. 
Land Ownership: Public Land Ownership: 119 lode mining claims, covering 2,230 acres.

Location: Additional Location Information: Located 3 miles southeast of Silver Peak (pop 213, 2022) in Clayton Valley, Nevada, adjacent to Albemarle’s active Silver Peak lithium mine. 
Project Description: Status of Project: The project received all necessary permits from the State of Nevada and the Nevada Division of Water Resources for the demonstration plant construction and water discharge in 2022 and 2023, respectively. Construction was largely completed by Q3 of 2023; The developer’s partner, SLB, demonstrated completion of specific technical milestones to qualify the earn-in to 100% Project ownership.  Those milestones included continuous production of lithium carbonate for an extended period and achieving a material quantity of lithium product in excess of a required purity threshold.  
Project Description: Regulatory Challenges: SLB’s subsidiary, NeoLith Energy, has plans for DLE in Clayton Valley and has sued Albemarle over water rights. State regulators have granted Silver Peak more than 20 “extensions of time” since the 1980s, though the state recently renewed a small temporary water permit for SLB’s pilot plant, recognizing that the Silver Peak mine has not used more than 70% of its water rights since 2022. But the state claims that no additional water allocations can be made, which puts Albemarle in a controlling position.  In 2024 the state renewed SLB’s water access permit but only for five years and only at a level sufficient to operate the DLE pilot plant. SLB and Partner Pure Energy Minerals now have all the permits they need to complete construction and operate the DLE demonstration plant. Water remains an issue for commercial-scale operation. 
Developer Description: Lead Developer: SLB (USA), oil services company, (formerly Schlumberger Technology Inc.) is both partner and operator of the Clayton Valley Project. On May 29, 2019, Pure Energy and SLB signed an earn-In agreement over the CV Project which requires significant investment by SLB at the Project, to include the design and construction of a pilot plant capable of processing lithium-bearing brines for high-quality lithium hydroxide monohydrate (“lithium hydroxide” or “LiOH∙H2O”) and/or lithium carbonate products at a specified rate.
Developer Description: Was There Change in Ownership during Project?: PEM acquired the Clayton NE claim blocks located in Esmeralda County from Advantage Lithium and Nevada Sunrise Gold under an asset purchase agreement made in November 2017.
Land Ownership: Type of Land: Public (BLM), 950 claims in Clayton Valley area, project area is 23,360 acres. 
Litigation: Evidence of Litigation: For several years, Pure Energy Minerals has challenged Albemarle’s claims to use most of the water in the Valley. In total, Albemarle has received 21 extensions since the 1980s, according to a recent filing from Pure Energy Minerals. In 2020, a Nevada state district court judge ruled against an extension for Albemarle's water rights.
Litigation: Court Rulings Issued: In August 2020, a district court judge sided with Pure Energy Minerals, remanding one of the extensions back to state regulators for further deliberations.

Location: Additional Location Information: Located 35 miles from Salmon (pop 3,295, 2023) in central Idaho at the site of the abandoned Canyon Salmon Mine. One mile from the confluence of the Main Salmon River and Middle Fork of the Salmon River.
Project Description: Existing Mine: Salmon Canyon Mine produced copper-cobalt-gold ore from 1964 to 1979 through underground methods.
Project Description: Status of Project: Koba Resources reports in its FY 2024 Annual Report that no significant work was done at its cobalt projects in FY 2024.
Concerned Interest Groups: Scale of Environmental Groups: Local -- Idaho Rivers United & Idaho Conservation League

Location: Additional Location Information: Near Tonopah, Nevada, 17 miles from Rhyolite Ridge                                                                                                                                             Project Description: Status of Project: January 2025: Completed an updated and comprehensive 3D geological and geophysical model for the Project, a major step forward in understanding the basin setting and the structural and lithological controls driving mineralization.  The Company is in the process of submitting an amended NOI with the BLM and additional borehole permits with the Nevada Division of Minerals (DMRE).                                                                                                                                                                                                   Project Description: Change in Ownership: In 2024 the developer completed the strategic acquisition of Altitude Ventures, secured CA$3.5M in financing, strengthened their corporate and technical teams, and obtained critical water rights and key permits.

Location: Additional Location Information: Existing facility adjacent to the Great Salt Lake in Ogden (pop 87,321, 2020), western Weber County, Utah. 
Project Description: Status of Project: The developer decided to delay indefinitely because the regulatory risks were too high, given Utah legislature concerns about water levels in Great Lake
Project Description: Regulatory Challenges: In 2023 Utah lawmakers passed HB513, which requires developers to pay a severance tax to a fund for the lake and makes them minimize water use and resupply water to the lake to offset their use.  The practical effect is that the developer must demonstrate that the project will not consume any water, as new state regulations limit water withdrawals from the Great Salt Lake. 
Financial Support: Public Supply Agreement w/ an Automaker or Battery/Component Producer: Binding five year agreement had been made with Ford for 40% of total production volume.
Concerned Interest Groups: Community Residents/Groups: Alliance for a Better Utah, which is a broad-based progressive advocacy group that works on issues ranging from health care and child care to environment. The alliance spearheaded legislation to limit use of water for brine operations, especially evaporation ponds.

Location: Additional Location Information: Located north of Montgomery and 50 miles south, southeast of Birmingham, and 23 miles south, southwest  of Sylacauga (pop 12,578, 2020), east-central Alabama. Mine site is in western Coosa County, adjacent to Talladega County.  A 37-mile swath of land known as the Graphite Belt runs entirely across Coosa County and into adjacent Alabama counties.
Project Description: Status of Project: Plan is for mine to open in 2027, processing facility sooner (broke ground in 2022).  
Commercial Plans: Processing Plan in US: New site in Coosa County.
Financial Support: Federal Agency: $3.2 million in DOD funding of feasibility study.  
Statements of Support from Public Officials: Local: Local city council.
Statements of Support from Public Officials: State: Alabama Governor and state senator support the project. 
Statements of Support from Public Officials: Federal: US Rep Mike Rogers.

Location: Additional Location Information: Located 43 miles northeast of Tucson, 10 miles from town of San Manuel (pop 3,551, 2010) and 6 miles from town of Mammoth (1,650, 2018 est), Arizona. 
Project Description: Mining Method: Open pit in the beginning, underground in second stage.
Project Description: Existing Mine: Began in early 1900s, changed ownership several times.  Abandoned mine purchased by Faraday Copper.
Project Description: Status of Project: BLM approved further drilling in May 2024; Building on its 2023 Preliminary Economic Assessment, the developer announced in May 2024 $15 million in private financing to move the project forward.
Developer Description: Was There Change in Ownership during Project?: Faraday Copper acquired the project in stages, 2018 and 2023.
Commercial Plans: Processing Done by the Same Lead Developer/Parent Company: Preliminary plan is to process onsite.
Land Ownership: Type of Land: Property includes seven private patented claims, one private land parcel, nine Arizona State Land Department (ASLD) prospecting permits and 325 Bureau of Land Management (BLM) unpatented mining claims
Concerned Interest Groups: Community Residents/Groups: Concerns over water usage and ineffective pollution monitoring systems.
Concerned Interest Groups: Indigenous Groups: San Carlos Apache Tribe.
Concerned Interest Groups: Scale of Environmental Groups: Local -- Save the Galiuro Mountains.
Reasons for Concern: Impacts to Natural Environment: Galiuro Mountains and Sonoran Desert, two popular recreation sites, are in vicinity of mine.
Reason for Concern: Water Quality: Impacts on Copper Creek, which empties into the San Pedro.
Reasons for Concern: Impact on Species: The project area currently serves as a migration corridor for wildlife. 
Reasons for Concern: Reputation of the Developer/Parent Company: Opposing group is concerned current developer will sell Copper Creek to large mining company with poor reputation for environmental protection and community engagement.
Reason for Concern: Other: Volatile boom bust cycle for community

Project Name: The developer is now using the name “Copper World Complex” to refer to a 44-year plan to mine on both sides of the mountains, an area that includes the former Rosemont project, the former Copper World project and additional private land the developer has acquired. 
Location: Additional Location Information:  Located approximately 30 miles southeast of Tucson in southern Arizona on Coronado National Forest land on the east slope of the Santa Rita Mountains. The nearest established communities are Sonoita (pop 803, 2020) and Vail (pop 13,604, 2020). The larger Copper World project includes land on the west slope of the Santa Ritas that was not part of the Rosemont Project.  
Project Description: Status of Project: The developer in 2023/2024 acquired the three necessary state permits: the Mined Land Reclamation Plan, the Aquifer Protection Permit, and the Air Quality Permit.  Phase 1 of the Copper World Complex, a 16-year plan, would develop the west side of the mountains with four open pits and three tailings dumps on approximately 4,500 acres of private land.  One of the flexible features of Phase 1 is that, since it does not use public land, the permits required would involve only the state of Arizona rather than the federal government.  To complete the Complex on the east side would require permits from the USFS. 
Project Description: Regulatory Challenges: Despite years of work and support from the State, the developer lost the Rosemont Project due to federal regulatory complications. The 9th Circuit ruled the developer may not dispose of waste material on adjacent public land, causing indefinite delay of the Rosemont project. 
Developer Description: Was There Change in Ownership during Project?:  Hudbay began purchasing shares of Augusta Resource Corporation of Canada in 2010.
Commercial Plans: Planned Production Capacity: Plan is to produce 1.5 million tons of copper over 15 years and 3.4 million tons over 28 years.  
Land Ownership: Type of Land: Public and Private- located partly within the Coronado National Forest near Tucson on 995 acres on private land, 75 acres of state-owned land, and 3,670 acres of mining claims on FS land.
Statements of Support from Public Officials: Federal: Several U.S. Senators supporting the Rosemont Mine sponsored a bill to overturn the 9th Circuit's decision but the bill could not attract enough support to pass the Senate. 
Statements of Concern from Public Officials: Local: In 2019 the Pima County Board of Supervisors, citing environmental concerns, narrowly passed a resolution opposing the mine. In 2022, some members of the City Council of Tucson registered concerns about water-storage issues related to the mine. 
Statements of Concern from Public Officials: Federal: The Army Corps of Engineers originally determined , during the Trump administration, that a clean water permit would be not necessary but the EPA, under the Biden administration, determined that a water permit would be necessary and the Army Corps reversed its position accordingly.
Litigation: Evidence of Litigation: A split 9th Circuit panel (2-1) upheld a district court ruling that the developer had established mineral prospects on only 300+ acres of Rosemont land but used an “in connection” with argument to allow waste and tailings to be discarded on nearby lands that have no demonstrated mineral potential.  The panel determined that no statute permits disposal of wastes on federal land without mineral deposits.  The US Supreme Court declined to hear an appeal..  
Concerned Interest Groups: Indigenous Groups: Hopi, Tohono O’odham and Pascua Yaqui Tribes.
Concerned Interest Groups: Scale of Environmental Groups: Local/Regional -- Sky Island Alliance, Save the Scenic Santa Ritas, Arizona Mining Reform Coalition; National -- Center for Biological Diversity, Earthjustice, Sierra Club.
Reasons for Concern: Site of Historical, Cultural, Spiritual Significance: Nearly 100 sacred and cultural sites of the Tohono O'odham Nation may be impacted by the proposed development in southern Arizona
Reasons for Concern: Other: Mistrust of state to monitor nearby aquifers; too much reliance on self monitoring by the developer.
Supportive Interest Groups: Commercial Groups: Arizona Mining Association; Southern Arizona Business Coalition. Tucson Business Association.

Location: County: The county is known for the Porcupine Mountains Wilderness State Park, affectionately called the Porkies, which spans about 60,000 acres. There’s North America’s largest ski jump, resorts, and the shore of Lake Superior.
Location: Additional Location Information: Located 14 miles and 24 miles from the towns of Wakefield (pop 1,702, 2020) and Ironwood (pop 5,045, 2020), respectively; at south edge of the Keweenaw Copper province, the Porcupine Mountains copper district, western end of upper peninsula of Michigan.
Project Description: Status of Project: Almost fully permitted, site preparation nearing the construction phase (pending project financing). The developer has projected construction start dates in the past that have not materialized. The latest information issued by the developer indicates the mine could open as soon as the spring of 2026.
Project Description: Regulatory Challenges: Permitting for the mine has sputtered for more than a decade, including multiple air quality permits from the state Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy. The last one expired in 2023; another proposal went out for public comment in late 2024.
Developer Description: Lead Developer: Owned 100%
Financial Support: Amount: The state (Michigan Strategic Fund) is currently considering a $50 million grant for infrastructure, conditional on the developer raising $150 million in private-sector support by December 2025.
Statements of Support from Public Officials: Local: The developer's supporters include many local governments, which believe the project will bolster the region’s economy.  Resolutions of support for the Copperwood Mine come from Gogebic County, Ontonagon County, the cities of Ironwood and Bessemer and Ironwood, Bergland, Carp Lake and Erwin townships and the Western Upper Peninsula Planning and Development Region Commission.
Statements of Support from Public Officials: State: Governor Gretchen Whitmer’s administration supports the project.
Concerned Interest Groups: Indigenous Groups: Anishinaabe People; Little Traverse Bay Bands of Odawa Indians
Concerned Interest Groups: Scale of Environmental Groups: Local -- Mining Action Group and Protect the Porkies. 
Concerned Interest Groups: Evidence of Organized Protest(s): Protests by tribes 
Reasons for Concern: Impacts to Natural Environment: The area is considered special because of the old-growth forests and proximity to the Porcupine Mountains, Wilderness State Park, and the shore of Lake Superior. 
Reasons for Concern: Traffic & Noise: Local residents express concerns about noise, light, and traffic.
Reasons for Concern: Subsistence Hunting/Fishing: The mine would be built on land Ojibwe nations ceded to the United States in the 1842 Treaty of La Pointe, stoking concerns that potential contamination could threaten the rights of Anishinaabe people to hunt, fish, and gather on ceded territory.
Reasons for Concern: Historical Mining or Reclamation Issues: Previous mining in the Keweenaw left dangerous reminders of the threat they can pose, like elements such as arsenic and mercury in wild rice beds in and around the Keweenaw Bay Indian Community reservation.
Reasons for Concern: Waste Management: The proposed site waste management plan includes a waste basin to store mining byproducts, sparking fears of potential leaks or ruptures that could threaten Lake Superior and nearby Presque Isle River.
Supportive Interest Groups: Commercial Groups: CEO of InvestUP, an economic development organization based in Marquette.
Reasons for Support: Economic Growth: Some see the project as a lifeline for the region’s struggling rural economy.  
Reasons for Support: Tax Revenue: $120 million in local, county and state tax revenue.
Reasons for Support: Employment: The Copperwood Mine would create 380 mining jobs. Spending from the mine, direct and indirect, would create an estimated 313 additional jobs.

Location: Additional Location Information: The Diamond Creek REE Project covers approximately 1,841 hectares (4,550 acres) and is comprised of 244 unpatented lode mining claims in central Idaho, a first tier mining jurisdiction located just north-northwest of the town of Salmon, Idaho.                                                                                               Project Description: Status of Project: Comprised of 4,550 acres of unpatented mining claims in the middle of the Idaho REE-Th Belt. Diamond Creek has a historic USGS resource which estimated 70,000+ tons of total rare earth elements at an average comprised ge grade of 1.22% TREO. In 2022 the company completed their first drill program at Diamond Creek, initial inspection of the core utilizing XRF analysis is favorable (see news release dated November 3rd) and are still awaiting the official assays from the lab.                     Land Ownership: Type of Land: Maintains 4,550 acres of unpatented mining claims and state lease land at Diamond Creek. :

Location: Additional Location Information: The mine is located in Western Marquette County, Upper Peninsula, Michigan; closest town is Big Bay (pop 257, 2020), 15 miles; Marquette (pop 20,629, 2020) is 33 miles away. Ore from the Eagle mine is trucked to the Humboldt mill, site of a former iron ore processing facility, for processing into concentrates. The Humboldt mill is approximately 37 miles west of Marquette.
Project Description: Status of Project: Only active nickel mine in the United States.  Production began 2014; shutdown scheduled for 2029 unless new reserves are discovered.
Project Description: Regulatory Challenges: From discovery of the deposit in 2003, it took almost 15 years before mining began. Environmental and indigenous groups mounted spirited opposition, including litigation. The Michigan Court of Appeals upheld the mine’s operating and water permits in August, 2013. 
Developer Description: Was There Change in Ownership during Project?: Lundin purchased Eagle Creek from Kennecott (Rio Tinto) in 2013.
Commercial Plans: Processing Plan in US: Processing at the  nearby Humboldt Mill.
Financial Support: Federal Agency:The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) has selected REV Nickel for an award up to $145 million. The REV Nickel Project, in partnership with Revex Technologies, will produce nickel concentrate and other valuable U.S.-sourced critical minerals from metal-bearing waste streams, including discarded mine tailings and spent lithium-ion batteries. The recipient of the this funding is not the developer of the mine.
Statements of Support from Public Officials: State: Former Governor Jennifer Granholm (D).
Statements of Support from Public Officials: Federal: Biden Administration.
Statements of Concern from Public Officials: Federal:  EPA.
Litigation: Evidence of Litigation: A coalition of national and local environmental groups and local tribes challenged both the state operating permit and the state water permit.  The litigation ended when the Michigan Court of Appeals affirmed both permits in August 2013. One lawsuit addressed that state operating permit; the other addressed the state water permit.
Concerned Interest Groups: Community Residents/Groups: Community Foundation of Marquette County
Concerned Interest Groups: Indigenous Groups: Prior to opening, the mine was a target of multiple protests by the Keweenaw Bay Indian Community (KBIC).
Concerned Interest Groups: Scale of Environmental Groups: National -- National Wildlife Federation (NWF); local/regional -- Mining Action Group (previously known as  Save the Wild U.P.) and Superior Watershed Partnership and Land Trust, Yellow Dog Watershed Preserve (YDWP); Upper Peninsula Environmental Coalition
Concerned Interest Groups: Recreational Groups: Huron Mountain Club (HMC); Snowmobile Club
Concerned Interest Groups: Evidence of Organized Protests: 2010 by Keweenaw Bay Indian Community
Reasons for Concern: Site of Historical, Cultural, Spiritual Significance: Eagle rock is a 60-foot outcrop next to the mine mouth that the Keweenaw Bay Indian Community tribe considers sacred.
Reason for Concern: Water Quality: Residents expressed fear that the sulfide mine will lead to sulfuric acid contamination of nearby water sources.
Reasons for Concern: Impact on Species: Unique Coaster Brook Trout.
Reasons for Concern: Subsistence Hunting/Fishing: Could threaten fish populations.
Reasons for Concern: Other: Structural issues and possible collapse of mine.

Location: Additional Location Information:  Located 3 miles west of Elk Creek (pop 67, 2020), and 6 miles south of Tecumseh (1,677, 2010), southeast Nebraska; 65 miles southeast of Lincoln (state capital) and 80 miles south of Omaha.
Project Description: Status of Project: Developer difficulties in raising funds to move to the development phase; May 2024 study found that electrification of mine could cut substantially both the capital and operating costs of the project.
Land Ownership: Type of Land: 622 staked mining claims covering approximately 6,871 hectares (16,975 acres) in northern Idaho, in four claim blocks.

Location: Additional Location Information: Located 9 miles northwest of the Blackbird Cobalt District in Idaho Cobalt Belt near Salmon (pop 3,295, 2023), central Idaho. 
Project Description: Existing Mine: Starting in 1921, ore with an average grade of 9.5% Co was regularly shipped from four mines in the area.
Project Description: Status of Project: Koba Resources reports in its FY 2024 Annual Report that no significant work was done at its cobalt projects in FY 2024.
Developer Description: Lead Developer: Koba Resources (Australia), spun off New World in 2021.
Developer Description: Was There Change in Ownership during Project?: Prior owner was New World Cobalt Limited (Australia), previously named Longford Resources (Australia); temporarily sold to Tyranna in August 2018. 
Land Ownership: Type of Land: 28 unpatented mining claims for 227 hectares of public land; part of Salmon National Forest (USFS)

Location: Additional Location Information:  Located in Cuyuna Iron Range near small town of Cuyuna (pop 296, 2020) in central Minnesota, 90 miles west of Duluth.
Project Description: Existing Mine: Mine closed in 1960, town of Harshaw was then abandoned.
Project Description: Status of Project: Exploratory drilling was completed in 2024, and the project is awaiting permits for further development.
Developer Description: Was There Change in Ownership during Project?: South32 purchased the land in 2018 from Arizona Mining.
Commercial Plans: Processing Plan in US: Processing either in Mexico or Canada.
Statements of Support from Public Officials: Federal: Designated FAST-41 for acelerated permitting during the Biden administration.
Concerned Interest Groups: Scale of Environmental Groups: Local -- Emily Mine Information Group
Reason for Concern: Water Quality: The aquifer that supplies drinking water to the town may be impacted by the mine.
Reason for Concern: Recreation: Mine may impact recreation in area, bird watching, and other tourism.
Reasons for Support: Historical Mining or Reclamation Issues: Developer assumed duty to clean up historical mining waste, completed in 2020, but some residents are still wary.
Supportive Interest Groups: Commercial Groups: Electrical cooperative named Crow Wing Power.

Location: Additional Location Information: Village of Dyer ~12 miles south; town of Tonopah ~50 miles east; northern Esmeralda County, equidistant (280 km) between Vegas and Reno, Fish Lake Valley, West Central Nevada.   Note: 30km northwest of Abermarle’s Silver Peak operations, 10km to Ioneer’s Rhyolite Ridge project, and 20km west of Argosy’s Tonopah Lithium project                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Project Description: Status of Project: A 2023 drilling program in north region suggests lithium brines likely in the south region.  January 2024 seismic reflection survey identifies promising drilling target in south region.  Next step is deep drill hole to a depth of 1,150 meters in the southern region.

Location: Additional Location Information: Located 4 miles south of Patagonia (pop 804, 2020) in southern Arizona, southern Patagonia Mountains, on ridge between Flux Canyon and Alum Gulch.
Project Description: Status of Project: The Flux Project was permitted for seven drill sites and, at this time (May 2024), has drilled on four of them. Remediation work has begun on both the new access roads and on the pads.  So far, the Flux Project has cut short access roads to four new pads, and finished drill work on them. Community outreach began in 2019.
Developer Description: Lead Developer: South 32 purchased Arizona Mining Inc.
Land Ownership: Type of Land: Coronado National Forest (USFS). 
Litigation: Evidence of Litigation: Eight local and national conservation groups  joined together to sue the Forest Service alleging the project's permits were wrongfully issued. The groups were represented by attorneys from EarthJustice. The Forest Service ultimately won the case. Local, regional and national environmental groups are now challenging the recent exploratory drilling permit issued by USFS.  Their quest for a preliminary injunction against drilling did not succeed in the courts, and the case was being heard on the merits as of late 2024.
Concerned Interest Groups: Scale of Environmental Groups: Patagonia Area Resource Alliance (PARA), Arizona Mining Reform Coalition, Center for Biological Diversity, Earthworks, Friends of Santa Cruz River, Friends of Sonoita Creek, Save the Scenic Santa Ritas, and Tucson Audubon Society,  Earthjustice, Western Mining Action Project
Reason for Concern: Impacts to Natural Environment: Concern is that Flux Project is one of several projects by different developers that could generate create “cumulative” ecological stress in the Patagonia Mountains area.
Reasons for Concern: Traffic & Noise: Noise levels could disrupt lives of species;  could lead to a flushing response in nesting Mexican spotted owls. Additionally, there are several other mining projects ongoing in the area, adding to the noise and traffic level.
Reasons for Concern: Classification of Species Impacted: Patagonia Mountains are home to endangered species like the Mexican spotted owl and Western yellow-billed cuckoo. The area is particularly important, advocates argue, for jaguars and ocelots migrating back and forth across the border with Mexico.  The Patagonia Mountains are believed to provide a corridor for jaguars and ocelots moving north from Mexico; they migrate through a border wall gap to their range in the United States. Recently a jaguar is believed to have traversed the Patagonia Mountains before being documented in the nearby Santa Rita Mountains. The mining projects may harm Harshaw Creek, a fragile riparian area teeming with biodiversity.
Supportive Interest Groups: Commercial Groups: The Southern Arizona Business Coalition and the Nogales-Santa Cruz County Chamber of Commerce

Location: Additional Location Information: Located in the Mojave Desert, CA, approximately 30 miles east of Barstow (pop 25,415, 2020) and two-and-four-tenths miles south of Interstate 40.
Project Description: Status of Project: Goal is to reach full production level in mid-2026. In 2023 the developer completed a Technical Report on capital costs for the full project. In 2024 the developer investigated federal funding opportunities at the Department of Defense and the Department of Energy.  In early January 2024 limited quantities of boric acid and lithium were extracted at four production wells.                                                                                                                                                                                            Developer Description: Lead Developer: When a group of investors acquired the Fort Cady project in 2016, the company, was known as American Pacific Borates, and was listed on the Australian Securities Exchange (ASX). It was later rebranded to 5E Advanced Materials and the primary listing was moved to the Nasdaq.                                                                                                                          
Commercial Plans: Planned Production Capacity: Phase 1 would yield around 1,100 tons per year of lithium carbonate, and this volume would be expected to rise to 5,500 tons per year in phase 3.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Commercial Plans: Total Capital Costs: Investment at the Fort Cady facility was $70 million as of mid-2023. Capital expenditures expected to be spread through 2024-26, totaling $373 million.
Financial Support: Grant/Loan: Some additional support from the US Department of Agriculture.

Location: Additional Location Information: Located near the township of Goodsprings (pop 162, 2020), southern Nevada, approximately 31 miles southwest of Las Vegas.
Project Description: Existing Mine: Long history of small-scale mining activity in Goodsprings district.
Project Description: Status of Project: Koba Resources reports in its FY 2024 Annual Report that no significant work was done at its cobalt projects in FY 2024. Soil sampling was done in 2018 by the site's previous owner, but no drilling has been conducted as of early 2025.
Developer Description: Was There Change in Ownership during Project?: The site was previously owned by New World Cobalt Limited (Australia), previously named Longford Resources. 
Land Ownership: Type of Land:The developer owns a 100% interest in 118 unpatented mining claims covering approximately 900 hectares.

Location: Additional Location Information: Located on the Seward Peninsula (Bering Strait), 35 miles north of town of Nome (pop 3,699, 2020), Alaska, near the Arctic Circle. 
Project Description: Status of Project: The developer announced in June 2024 a field program for 2024 that would collect the required data, including additional drilling, for a prefeasibility study, which is expected to be completed in early 2025.
Project Description: Regulatory Challenges: Most of the permitting will be handled by the State of Alaska.  However, the project necessitates the construction of a road network to the property (e.g., a new road network through the Arctic from Nome to the mine site).   A previous effort to obtain the federal wetlands permit from the Corps was not successful. In 2018 local community and environmental opposition led to a delay in the Corps deliberations and a temporary loss of state funding for the project. The developer is expected to make another effort to obtain the federal wetlands permit.  
Commercial Plans: Processing Plan in US: Processing to be conducted in Niles, Ohio.
Financial Support: Federal Agency: DOD grant of $37.5 million.  However, the grant has led to a consultation controversy.  Three tribal governments (Telles, Brevig Mission, anermit;  In 2018 local community opposition to the road network led to a temporary loss of state funding and diminished prospects for the Army Corps pd Mary Igloo) stated in December 2023 that the Biden Department of Defense violated its own consultation principles when it awarded the $37.5 million grant to the developer for the proposed graphite mine in Alaska.  The grant was announced in July 2023 but DOD never responded to three independent letters from the three tribes.  In December 2023 the tribes disclosed the letters, which were written with the assistance of the environmental law firm Trustees for Alaska.
Concerned Interest Groups: Scale of Environmental Groups: Local -- Northern Alaska Environmental Center
Reason for Concern: Water Quality: Proximity of mining site to important water sources is reportedly a cause for concern in nearby communities.
Reasons for Concern: Subsistence Hunting/Fishing: Native Americans near the project site practice traditional food-gathering practices that they believe may be affected by the mine.
Supportive Interest Groups: Commercial Groups: Bering Straits Native Corp.
Reasons for Support: Employment: 300 jobs to be created in rural Alaska.

Location: Additional Location Information: Paradox Basin, 20 miles northwest of Moab, Grand County, southeastern Utah; 13 miles northwest of Intrepid Potash’s evaporation pond solution mining operation. The proposed exploration area is located approximately 21 miles northwest of the town of Moab, Utah and 27 miles southeast of the town of Green River, Utah in the Spring Canyon Point area between the geographic features of Spring Canyon and Ten Mile Wash that are adjacent to the Green River.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Project Description: Co-Producing Materials: Wells in and around our project reported lithium up to 500ppm, bromine up to 6,100 ppm and boron up to 1,260 ppm (Gilbride & Santos, 2012). This data is reinforced by nearby potash production and the advanced stage of neighbouring lithium projects.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 Project Description: Land Ownership: Federal and State. The developer holds a 100% interest in eleven State of Utah (SITLA) mineral and minerals salt leases covering approx. 7,050 acres, 1095 federal lithium brine claims (Bureau of Land Management ("BLM") Placer Claims) covering 21,150 acres, and 11 federal (BLM) potash prospecting permits covering approximately 25,480 acres. Through these leases, permits and claims the Company has the ability to explore for potash, lithium and potential by-products across the entire Green River Project (approx. 32,530 acres).                                                                                                                       Project Description: Change in Ownership: In 2009, American Potash entered into an option
agreement with Sweetwater River Resources for interest in these PPAs and was established as the Operator by the BLM in 2012. In 2024 a  new option agreement with LiK Resources LLC, a private Houston-based exploration company, on its Green River Potash and Lithium Project; the agreement defines conditions for 70% ownership by LiK Resources.

Location: Additional Local Information: Near Green River (pop 827, 2020), a small community along Interstate 70, in Emery County, southeastern Utah. The Green River lithium project, which abuts the Green River, is located 32 miles from the same developer’s Paradox lithium project.                                                                                                            Statement of Concern: Federal:  Federal agencies, including the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) and Bureau of Reclamation, later voiced concerns over the project — the BLM said the application was premature because the company hadn’t yet sought its approval to operate on federal land. Reclamation worried the project would withdraw water from the beleaguered Colorado River.
