Plus, the company had “not provided sufficient information to demonstrate that water returned to the hydrologic system following mineral extraction would not contaminate or otherwise affect nearby water sources or downstream users,” the bureau wrote to the Utah Division of Water Rights.                                                       Litigation: Evidence of Litigation: Lawsuit filed In Utah’s 7th District Court in Moab against the Utah Division of Water Rights by environmental groups and nearby residents. The lawsuit claims that decision should be invalidated because the project could impair existing water rights, while interfering with “the more beneficial use of the water.” The company also hasn’t filed “a contract for payment of royalties” which is required by the state, the complaint alleges. And, the project is “detrimental to the public welfare,” with the lawsuit arguing the state is unable “to assess the legitimacy of Blackstone’s claims related to direct lithium extraction and its impacts on water consumption and water rights.”     Concerned Interest Groups: Scale of Environmental Groups: Local/Regional.  Living Rivers and the Great Basin Water Networks.
Concerned Interest Groups: Recreational Groups: Tourism.  Holiday River Expeditions, a guiding operation based in Green River.

Project Name: The Halleck Creek Project was recently renamed the Cowboy State Mine, see Project Note on Developer.   
Location: Additional Location Information: Located in Laramie Mountains, southeast Wyoming; closest town is Wheatland (population 3,500, 2020). 
Project Description: Co-Producing Materials: Neodymium, praseodymium, dysprosium, and terbium, as well as secondary magnetic rare-earth oxides (REOs).  There is also a possibility that the Brook deposit may contain meaningful amounts of gallium and germanium, two critical minerals that are widely used in semiconductors and defense systems.
Project Description: Status of Project: 2024 drilling program confirmed enormous potential of the project. Developer is advancing toward completing an updated resource estimate and Pre-Feasibility Study (PFS).                                                                                                                                             
Developer Description: Lead Developer: A restructuring occurred in 2024 to attract domestic investment, accelerate development, and ease issues with foreign investment rules. Wyoming Rare Inc.is now separate and 100% owned; American Rare Earths is the parent organization. The company partitioned the Cowboy State Mine section of its Halleck Creek project into an independent entity now called Wyoming Rare (USA) Inc., or WRI, which may help the project draw on a targeted class of investors.
Financial Support: Federal Agency: In late 2024, the Export-Import Bank of the United States (EXIM) issued a non-binding Letter of Interest to provide up to US$456 million in debt financing to the project, specifically to assist with construction and operations of the project. Developer, Wyoming Rare Inc, also received $304,000 from the Wyoming Energy Authority as apart of their grant program.
Land Ownership: Type of Land: 4,500 acres were permitted for mining in 2020; 15,800 acres in total

Location: Additional Location Information: Located near Nogales (pop 19,770, 2020) in the abandoned mining district of Harshaw, Patagonia Mountains, southern Arizona; 50 miles southeast of Tucson, 20 miles from US-Mexican border.
Project Description: Status of Project: In January 2024 the developer released the Critical Minerals Exploration and Mine Plan of Operations, a roadmap of operational activities at the Hermosa project from start to finish, as the project is located on lands managed by the Coronado National Forest. Later in 2024, the developer secured from the state a key air quality permit.
Project Description: Regulatory Challenges: The USFS approved a 15-hole exploration plan in October 2011.  Under litigation pressure from wildlife and conservation groups, USFS withdrew approval of the exploration plan in April 2012. The developer and USFS then worked for several years on a revised environmental assessment. 
Developer Description: Was There Change in Ownership during Project?: Acquired Phelps-Dodge in 2007.
Commercial Plans: Planned Lifespan of Mine: Estimated Mine Life: 2056
Financial Support: Federal Agency: $20M federal support from DOD under the Defense Production Act Battery Program. DOE providing $166M, or up to one third of the cost of the manganese production facility at the Hermosa mine.  
Land Ownership: Type of Land: Purchased from the BLM: In September 2005, as part of a "land swap", Phelps Dodge (which was subsequently purchased by Freeport-McMoran) transferred 3,867 acres of "environmentally sensitive" land to the BLM and purchased 16,297 acres located next to proposed mine from the BLM. In order to reach full production, the mine must also obtain approval from USFS because of proximity to a national forest.  That process is underway.
Statements of Concern from Public Officials: Local: Mayor of Patagonia has stated that the town does not support the mine
Litigation: Evidence of Litigation: A federal district court has ordered the Forest Service to complete a Supplemental Information Report and consider another report under the National Environmental Policy Act; the court gave both parties a schedule of deadlines extending through April 2025. Both the district court and the 9th Circuit denied requests from environmentalists to halt exploratory drilling while litigation against USFS exploratory permit is resolved. 
Concerned Interest Groups: Scale of Environmental Groups: Local -- Patagonia Area Resource Alliance (PARA), Sky Island Alliance, Friends of Sonoita Creek; National -- Earthworks, Defenders of Wildlife; Center for Biological Diversity.
Reasons for Concern: Water Supply: Possible dverse effect of groundwater pumping on the Gila or nearby springs and Bonita Creek
Reasons for Concern: Impact on Species: Concerns about ocelot, Mexican spotted owl, Pima pineapple cactus; jaguar. 
Reasons for Support: Economic Growth: This project could be the largest single investment in the history of Santa Clara County.

Location: Additional Location Information: Located approximately 40 miles west of Salmon (pop 3,295, 2023) in the Salmon-Challis Forest near Cobalt (pop 13, 2020), central Idaho. The site is adjacent to the inactive Blackbird mine. 
Project Description: Status of Project: 2024 drilling program confirmed promise of the Ram deposit.                                                                                                                                                                        
Concerned Interest Groups: Indigenous Groups: Shoshone-Bannock Tribes, whose historic homeland covers the southern half of Idaho and large portions of bordering states.
Concerned Interest Groups: Scale of Environmental Groups: Local/Regional -- Idaho Conservation League.

Project Name: The Idaho Cobalt Project is made up of the Victory Project, the Fairway Project, the Twin Peaks Project, and the Ulysses Project
Location: Additional Location Information: The Idaho Cobalt Project is comprised of two operations in separate locations in Idaho; the Mine and Mill, and the Cobalt Production Refining Facility (CPF). The Mine and Mill site is in East Central Idaho, approximately 26 miles west of the town of Salmon (pop 3,295, 2023). The CPF site is in an industrial park in the Blackfoot municipal area (pop 12,346, 2020) in southwest Idaho.  
Project Description: Co-Producing Materials: Idaho stands as one of the three locations globally, along with Finland and Morocco, where cobalt is the primary metal, making it a highly exceptional region for cobalt resources. However, the projects also would produce some copper and gold, which should enhance the economic viability of the projects.
Project Description: Existing Mine: Historical Twin Peaks mine and former Badger prospect. 
Project Description: Status of Project: The developer in 2023-2024 undertook geological mapping and rock sampling, combined  with a river sediment sampling program in the Twin Peaks area.  
Developer Description: Lead Developer: The lead developer, Champion Electric Metals, was established in 2016 under the name “Idaho Champion”, since initially it focused solely on Idaho-centric assets. However, in 2023 the company rebranded to Champion Electric to reflect its expansion into Québec and their focus on battery metals.
Land Ownership: Type of Land: 6,280 acres of public land in Salmon National Forest

Location: Additional Location Information: Located 3 miles east of Grimes Pass (pop 192, 2020), 14 miles north of Idaho City,  40 miles northwest of Boise, southern Idaho.
Project Description: Mining Method: Open-pit.
Project Description: Co-Producing Materials: Molybdenum is an important metal used primarily in high-quality steel applications, for strength, corrosion resistance and other properties. Since molybdenum prices are roughly 5 times the price of copper, and the developer expects that somewhat equivalent volumes of both metals will be produced, molybdenum may provide the bulk of the revenue generated. Silver will contribute a much smaller share of the revenue.  The ore at CuMo also contains recoverable rhenium (a defense metal) and tungsten.
Project Description: Status of Project: Exploration. USFS decision on Plan of Operations due 2025, which would facilitate more exploratory drilling.Most of the previous exploration was done between the late 1990s and 2012, the year of the last drilling. The developer started a Preliminary Economic Assessment in 2024, completion is due 1Q 2025.  
Project Description: Regulatory Challenges: The Project has a complex regulatory history, even though the developer has not yet completed exploration. The original USFS environmental assessment lost in court in 2012 to a lawsuit by environmental groups.  The prior owner then moved the Project through a Supplemental Environmental Assessment (SEA) that concluded in October 2015 with a Finding of No Significant Impact and a favorable Decision Notice from USFS on exploratory drilling. But, USFS is now redoing the SEA because of another judicial reversal and submission of a new plan by the current developer.  The new plan contains environmental protection measures such as dust abatement and all roads are located at least 500 feet slope distance from perennial streams such as Grimes Creek.  Special measures in the plan include spill containment, which the plan said will be provided at all gasoline-powered pumps near streams or water sources. The drill systems will also operate on a “closed system,” meaning fluids are mixed at the drill site, sent directly down the drill pipe, and return fluids recirculate back up the hole. The plan said the fluid products are non-toxic or biodegradable. The developer will also monitor surface and groundwater, and will continue to analyze and study LESA (Sacajawea’s bitterroot), ensuring the overall population will not be threatened or endangered during project operations. Even if USFS approves the plan, more litigation seems likely.  
Developer Description: Was There Change in Ownership during Project?: IC separated from American CuMo Mining Corporation in 2018.
Commercial Plans: Planned Production Capacity: Projected initial yearly copper output through a sulfide concentrator may be in the range of 30 million pounds, molybdenum up to 50 million pounds, with about a million ounces of silver.   
Land Ownership: Type of Land: Public (USFS), located in Boise National Forest.  The project currently consists of 126 federal unpatented lode mining claims, and 6 patented mining claims. In total, the project comprises approximately 2,640 acres.
Litigation Evidence of Litigation: In 2012, the U.S. District Court for the District of Idaho found that the Forest Service had not adequately analyzed the groundwater issues associated with exploration.  he USFS revised the environmental analysis and approved the exploration plan again in 2015.  In the supplemental environmental assessment, USFS and the developer decided to go with an alternative B project which was a “reduced roads” option, intended to address concerns over potential erosion and sedimentation to Grimes Creek. Grimes Creek feeds into Mores Creek, which feeds into Lucky Peak Reservoir. Three environmental organizations filed another lawsuit in early 2016. This time, the court said that the Forest Service had adequately looked at groundwater impacts and had addressed the Idaho Department of Environmental Quality’s concerns about degraded water quality, but did no not adequately determine the impacts on Sacajawea’s bitterroot (a rare, beautiful plant that occurs only in central Idaho).  
Concerned Interest Groups: Scale of Environmental Groups: Local/Regional -- Idaho Conservation League, Idaho Rivers United, Advocates for the West, and Golden Eagle Audubon
Reasons for Concern: Impacts to Natural Environment: Environmental groups are concerned that the developer's exploration activities, including road building, may impact Grimes Creek and the South Fork Payette River, which is eligible to be protected under the Wild and Scenic Rivers Act.  They are also concened that scenic values will be compromised, since roads and construction would be visible from the river corridor near Danskin. The ultimate concern is the mine itself, if constructed, would hurt the amazing scenery that the South Fork is currently known for.    
Reasons for Concern: Water Quality: The Boise River is the lifeblood of the Treasure Valley. The exploration site is upstream of half of Idaho’s population, and the Boise River watershed provides approximately 30 percent of Boise’s drinking water supply and irrigates over 300,000 acres of farmland. In the eyes of environmental groups and some community residents, the proposal places the entire watershed – and all who rely on it – at unacceptable risk.
Reasons for Concern: Classification of Species Impacted: Environmental groups are also concerned that the forest habitat of endangered species could be disrupted.  The Project site includes some of the best forest habitat remaining in the Boise Basin for an array of wildlife, including sensitive species like great grey owl, American goshawk, and wolverine. The exploration area also hosts a rare flower found only in the mountains of central Idaho, Sacajawea’s bitterroot. 
Reasons for Concern: Subsistence Hunting/Fishing: Recreation and fisheries are also areas of concern.  The surrounding watershed provides habitat for bull trout and native redband trout. If there is an increase in sedimentation, fish populations within and downstream of the project area may be adversely impacted.

Location: Additional Location Information: Located about 18 miles southwest of Salmon (3,295, 2023) in central Idaho, within the historic Blackbird cobalt-copper district of the Idaho Cobalt Belt. Iron Creek is a tributary creek that drains from the Salmon River Mountains in the west into the Salmon River. The Property encompasses the North Fork of Iron Creek.  
Project Description: Status of Project: In November 2024 the developer acquired a 10-year permit from the USFS for exploration in and around its Iron Creek project at the eastern end of the Idaho Cobalt Belt. The developer has planned more drilling activities outside of the current resource area over the next two years. The Preliminary Economic Assessment is anticipated to begin shortly (June 2024).
Developer Description: Lead Developer: Formerly known as First Cobalt Corp, Electra purchased Iron Creek Property in 2018.
Commercial Plans: Planned Production Capacity: The planned production level from the Ontario refinery is 6,500 metric tons per year of battery-grade cobalt sulfate per year.  But not all of that output will come from mined material from the Iron Creek Project.  
Commercial Plans: Processing Plan Elsewhere in North America: The developer's Ontario Cobalt Refinery may become one of the world's lowest carbon sources of battery-grade cobalt due to the hydrometallurgical process used and the clean hydroelectricity powering the facility.
Financial Support: Federal Agency: In August 2024, the U.S. Department of Defense (DOD) awarded the developer $20 million to complete the construction and commissioning of North America's only refinery capable of producing cobalt sulfate, along with other materials needed for lithium-ion batteries. The developer also has a grant from the Canadian government. In June 2024, NRCan invested $3.6 million toward a battery materials recycling plant being built alongside the Ontario Cobalt Refinery. This recycling operation will be able to recover high-quality lithium, nickel, cobalt, manganese, and graphite from black mass, a powder-like material produced when lithium-ion batteries are shredded for recycling.
Financial Support: Public Supply Agreement w/ an Automaker or Battery/Component Producer: In July  2023, the developer announced that its battery-grade cobalt sulfate agreement with LG Energy Solution, a leading global manufacturer of lithium-ion batteries, had been extended and expanded from the initial terms. The agreement now provides for the supply of 19,000 tonnes of cobalt contained in sulfate beginning in 2025. The total will represent up to 80% of the developer's expected annual production.
Concerned Interest Groups: Scale of Environmental Groups: Local -- Idaho Conservation League

Location: Additional Location Information: Located near Kings Mountain (pop 11,142, 2020), 35 miles west of Charlotte, North Carolina. Most of the town is in Cleveland County, with a small eastern portion in Gaston County.  The project site is off Interstate 85.
Project Description: Existing Mine: The lithium mine at King’s Mountain, North Carolina operated from 1938 to 1988; Foote Mineral closed the mine in 1988 without a reclamation plan; Site was abandoned in 1980s as low-cost South American lithium dominated the global market.
Project Description: Status of Project: Exploratory drilling began in 2017; the developer has drilled more than 300,000 feet of core across the property. The developer has invested approximately $100 million over the last five years in studies and testing to determine the commercial promise of the site; The developer's original plan was to restart the mine in 2026 but that plan has been delayed due to the lithium-price slump and financial issues. Nonetheless, in September 2024, the developer submitted applications for several state and federal permits that are required to relaunch mining at Kings Mountain.
Developer Description: Lead Developer: Albemarle acquired the site in 2015. The developer (Albemarle) is a large global specialty chemicals company.  Its lithium business includes lithium through its own salt brine assets in Chile and the United States and two joint venture interests in hard-rock Australian mines, Talison (Greenbushes) and Wodgina.  It is developing additional lithium mines in the US and Argentina.The recent collapse of global lithium prices has caused Albemarle to lay off employees and curb capital spending in both 2023 and 2024. 
Developer Description: Was There Change in Ownership during Project?: The developer purchased the abandoned site in 2015.  
Commercial Plans: Planned Production Capacity: Newly estimated annual volume of production is 420,000 tonnes, which is drastically larger than the previous 50,000 ton output. The new estimate comes after the proposed mine was expanded 900 feet southwest of its previous position. 
Commercial Plans: Processing Done by the Same Lead Developer/Parent Company:The developer currently operates a lithium processing facility at Kings Mountain with a production capacity of 5,500 tons per year. The developer also announced plans to create a “mega-flex” lithium conversion facility in the U.S. Southeast that would process up to 100,000 tons of lithium per year. The Kings Mountain mine would provide roughly half the raw material for the new plant.
Financial Support: Federal Agency: The $90 million grant from DOD is unusual because it can be used to pay the costs of reopening the mine, especially mining equipment.
Financial Support: Grant/Loan: In October 2022 the developer received a $150 million grant from DOE for processing facility site development, for the company's expanding Silver Peak Mine in Nevada, and for training/research in Cleveland, Ohio and Raleigh North Carolina. At King's Mountain, the funds will pay a portion of the cost of a new commercial scale lithium concentrator facility 
Statements of Support from Public Officials: Local: Mayor of King's Mountain is a proponent of the Project.                          
Concerned Interest Groups: Community Residents/Groups: In March 2022, a series of town halls were hosted in nearby communities by the developer to help the company decide whether to reopen the mine; Some community residents expressed concern, but fewer – and with less intensity – than were expressed at the nearby Piedmont Lithium site. A homeowner at Kings Mountain refused to sell his land to the developer, and claims that his home begins shaking each time the developer engages in any blasting.  The developer states that there has been no blasting near the resident's home.  
Reasons for Concern: Air Quality: Dust emissions from mining and trucks are a concern among residents. 
Reasons for Concern: Water Quality: Arsenic is naturally occurring around lithium deposits and around the King’s Mountain site; a concern is that the arsenic could be released during construction or mining and leak into surface or groundwater.  At other sites, mining has been associated with contamination of drinking water wells.
Reasons for Concern: Recreation: Reopening the mine would require rerouting a hiking trail.

Location: Additional Location Information: Located 16 miles northeast of Boise (pop 707, 2020), and 66 miles northwest of Phoenix, Arizona.
Project Description: Status of Project: All necessary construction permits (state, local & federal) have been secured; The developer’s 2024 communications suggest it is giving higher priority to the Halleck Creek opportunity than to the La Paz Project.  
Commercial Plans: Processing Done by the Same Lead Developer/Parent Company: Hydrometallurgical Plant and Pyrometallurgical Plant are both planned for the site.
Financial Support: Federal Agency: In-kind assistance through collaboration with DOE’s Critical Material Institute; no grant or loan
Land Ownership: Type of Land: Project covers 6866 acres; it includes the Beaver Creek and Searchlight properties. $300 million in royalties to be paid to landowners.
Statements of Support from Public Officials: State: Nebraska Governor Pete Ricketts nominated the Elk Creek Project as a “National High-Priority Infrastructure” Project to the White House.
Statements of Concern from Public Officials: Local: Not organized (yet) but there are local concerns over management of radioactive material.
Supportive Interest Groups: Commercial Groups: Arizona State Land Trust, the Arizona Commerce Commission, the La Paz Economic Development Corporation, the Genesee and Wyoming Railroad Group.

Location: Additional Location Information: Located near Pahrump (pop 44,738, 2022) on the border of Nevada and California near the Mojave Desert; on the edge of Ash Meadow National Wildlife Refuge in southern Nevada, about 70 miles northwest of Las Vegas. 
Project Description: Status of Project: In March 2024 the developer launched environmental baseline surveys as it grapples with some tenacious opposition to its request for an exploratory drilling permit. 
Project Description: Regulatory Challenges: A permit for exploratory drilling was granted but then revoked due to environmental (water-related) concerns raised jointly by county officials and an environmental group.  A more limited exploration plan was then submitted by the developer, and is under review by BLM. Meanwhile, County officials are trying to persuade the Department of Interior and the Congress to withdraw nearby lands from development activity due to environmental concerns.       
Land Ownership: Type of Land: Developer acquired an additional 2,400 acres that allowed abandonment of certain existing mining claims that border the ACEC boundary of Ash Meadows. This moves the core of the LGL project further away from Ash Meadows and sends a clear message that the developer is committed to developing the project in a manner that is sustainable for the surrounding area.
Statements of Concern from Public Officials: Local: Unincorporated town of Beatty has a concern over invasive activity so close to a declared refuge.
Litigation: Evidence of Litigation: The Center for Biological Diversity and the Amargosa Conservancy sued BLM for failing to consult with other federal agencies such as the US Fish and Wildlife Service concerning species protection under the Endangered Species Act. The lawsuit was not resolved because BLM withdrew its initial approval of the drilling plan. 
Concerned Interest Groups: Scale of Environmental Groups: National -- Center for Biological Diversity; Local/Regional -- Amargosa Conservancy. 
Reasons for Concern: Impacts to Natural Environment: Adjacent to Ash Meadows National Wildlife Refuge.
Reasons for Concern: Water Supply: County concerned about mine's consumption of scarce water
Reasons for Concern: Classification of Species Impacted: Environmental groups are concerned that 26 unique species are potentially threatened by the mine. Some of the proposed drill sites are within 2,000 feet of Fairbanks Spring, a critical habitat for the endangered Ash Meadows Amargosa pupfish.

Location: Additional Location Information: The facility is planned for somewhere on the Promontory Point peninsula, near Brigham City (19,650, 2020), Utah, on the Great Salt Lake’s saltier northern arm.
Project Description: Status of Project: Lilac Solutions released a technical white paper in June 2024 showing that its new DLE technology has 50% lower capital costs than previously estimated and longer durability (4,000 cycles).  The company also predicted that its pilot plant at Great Salt Lake will be running in October 2024. The company's plan is to scale up commercial operations to extract 3,000 tons of lithium from the lake annually by 2026. 
Project Description: Regulatory Challenges: The State of Utah placed a moratorium on water withdrawals from the Great Salt Lake. 
Financial Support: Federal Agency: $50 m from DOE for a commercial-scale DLE demonstration plant
Financial Support: Public Supply Agreement w/ an Automaker or Battery/Component Producer: Binding five year agreement with Ford for 40% of total production volume. In 2024 Lilac reported $145 million in new private financing, which will go toward scaling operations. 
Statements of Support from Public Officials: Federal: Lawmakers passed HB513 in 2023, which requires mineral extraction firms to pay a severance tax to a fund for the Lake and compels them to minimize water use and resupply water to the Lake to offset their use
Concerned Interest Groups: Scale of Environmental Groups: Regional -- Great Basin Water Network

Location: Additional Location Information: Located near Wendover (pop 1,115, 2020), western Utah;  105 miles west of Salt Lake City along Highway 80. Property is located south of the Pilot Valley, at the western margin of the Bonneville Salt Flats.
Project Description: Mining Method: Extraction from brines. 
Project Description: Existing Mine:Three abandoned oil drilling operations. 
Project Description: Status of Project: Developer has made additional claims to avoid floodplain areas.  Plans for exploratory drilling underway in 2024. 
Developer Description: Lead Developer: Global Battery Minerals (Canada) acquired the property in 2021 
Land Ownership: Type of Land: Public (BLM).  7,900 acres of placer claims.

Location: Additional Location Information: Located near village of Cobalt (262, 2023) and Fredericktown (pop 4,429, 2020), Missouri, 90 miles south of St. Louis.
Project Description: Existing Mine: Abandoned: mine was originally discovered in 1847 and has since undergone various periods of operation and closure.  Production started 1944.  Peak production 1983. Surface and underground operations. Now an EPA Superfund site.
Project Description: Status of Project: The developer is establishing partnership agreements as it presses its case for financial support from the federal government. Glencore added a processing partnership with US Strategic Metals and a Chilean company in 2024, along with the 2022 partnership with United States Strategic Metals LLC.
Developer Description: Was There Change in Ownership during Project?:  Missouri Cobalt purchased land in 2018.
Commercial Plans: Processing Done by the Same Lead Developer/Parent Company: Constructing nickel/cobalt processing facility that will produce battery-grade material.
Financial Support: Federal Agency: $100.8 Million loan, now in expedited approval process, from the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services in recognition of the potential job creation by the company’s critical minerals project. 
Litigation: Evidence of Litigation: 2024 lawsuit against Missouri Cobalt by DOJ/EPA alleges pollution of nearby bodies with copper and lead without permit.
Reason for Concern: Air Quality: Community concerned about waste from the refining process, which may use carcinogenic chemicals to separate the cobalt.

Location: Additional Location Information: Southeast margin of the Highland Mountains, 1 mile west of Silver Star (pop 46, 2020) and 16 miles south of Whitehall (pop 1,006, 2020), Madison County, southwest Montana.

Location: Additional Location Information: Located 5 miles west of Yerington (pop 3,194, 2023), in central-western Nevada near the California line; approximately 47 miles southeast of Reno.
Project Description: Mining Method: Traditional open pit shovel/truck operation.
Project Description: Existing Mine: The Mason Valley property hosted several historical underground copper mines that were in production in the early 1900s. Historical drilling and production records from the past producing mines indicate the mineralization is high grade and starts at or near surface.    
Project Description: Status of Project: The developer views the Mason project as a long-term development asset and a high-quality copper growth opportunity. . Since acquiring Mason, the developer has consolidated mining claims contiguous to the project and advanced technical studies, including a revised resource model and a PEA.  In September 2023 a drill program was launched to test satellite deposits which confirmed the occurrence of high-grade skarn mineralization near the historical mines; they are potentially amenable to open pit mining but of limited spatial extent. In 2024 the developer was compiling and analyzing the results from the 2023 drilling and conducting additional metallurgical studies to refine Project economics.  No definite timetable has been disclosed for opening the mine.
Developer Description: Was There Change in Ownership during Project?: The developer purchased Mason Resources including the Mason Project in December 2018.  The developer consolidated a prospective package of patented and unpatented mining claims contiguous to the Mason project in two private transactions in 2019 and 2020, including a property called Mason Valley. Much of the Mason Valley property is located on Hudbay’s wholly owned private lands and contains highly prospective skarn mineralization. 
Commercial Plans: Planned Production Capacity: 140,000 tons per yeat for the first 10 years declining thereafter
Commercial Plans: Processing Plan in US: A new nearby copper sulphide mineral processing plant capable of producing commercial grade copper and molybdenum concentrate. 
Land Ownership: Type of Land: Private, more land added in 2019 and 2020.

Location: Additional Location Information: Located 35 km (x 0.62 for miles) west of the town of McDermitt (pop 124, 2020), Nevada, at the northern tip of Nevada on the Oregon border.
Project Description: Mining Method: Open pit method processing ore using sulphation roasting to produce battery-grade lithium carbonate.
Project Description: Status of Project: The developer is completing technical and financial studies to support a new resource estimate and update metallurgical understanding; A pre-feasibility study was in progress in 2024.
Developer Description: Was There Change in Ownership during Project?: The developer acquired the Project in 2018. By 2023 a total of 62 drill holes had supported increasing Mineral Resource Estimates.
Processing Plan: Processing Done by the Same Lead Developer/Parent Company: Developer envisions an open pit mining operation that processes ore onsite using sulphation roasting to produce battery-grade lithium carbonate. The developer is partnering with POSCO Holdings on tests of processing methods.
Land Ownership: Type of Land: Project encompasses 7,200 acres (BLM) and would require the construction of 30.2 miles of new access routes
Statements of Support from Public Officials: State: Applications to DOE and DOD for federal financial support include supporting statements from leading political officials in Oregon
Concerned Interest Groups: Indigenous Groups: Nearest town is 75% Native American, Northern Paiute and Shoshone
Concerned Interest Groups: Scale of Environmental Groups: Local -- Oregon Natural Desert Association 
Reasons for Concern: Site of Historical, Cultural, Spiritual Significance: Concern over impacts to tribal culture
Reasons for Concern: Classification of Species Impacted: Sage Grouse (endangered); Lahontan Cutthroat Trout (threatened)
Reason for Support: Employment: 600 jobs created

Project Description: Additional Location Information: Location: 34 miles west of the town of Tonopah (2,009, 2021), Esmeralda County, Nevada; southeast of Albemarle’s Silver Peak Mine                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   Project Descrption: Status of Project: Spearmint is currently permitted by the BLM for 4 additional drill holes on the McGee Lithium Clay Project, building on its 2022 drilling on the property.  The 2022 drilling assessed the lithium resource potential west of the lithium mineral resource, building on the 2021 drilling program  which discovered a continuous, well mineralized section from near surface to a maximum depth of approximately 900 ft (274 m) below surface.                                                                                            Land Ownership: Type of Land: The Project consists of 26 contiguous unpatented placer claims that span from McGee 30 to McGee 55 and cover 890 acres.

Location: Additional Location Information: Located in the Duluth Complex (rock formation), near the towns of Babbitt (pop 1,383, 2020) and Hoyt Lakes (pop 2,020, 2020), northeastern Minnesota; about one mile from site for PolyMet project. 
Project Description: Existing Mine: Site is a former iron mine, and adjacent to iron mines that are still operating.
Project Description: Status of Project: In August 2024 the developer announced four new studies to enhance the sustainability of the project.  The study topics include tailings storage, water science, efficient production, and carbon reduction. The developer continues to invest in studies for the Mesaba project’s environmental and social baseline studies and complete expanded hydrologic and hydrogeological studies.  Ongoing work also addresses orebody knowledge and project development engineering options.
Developer Description: Lead Developer: New Range Copper Nickel LLC is a 50/50 joint venture established by Teck Resources and Glencore to develop the NorthMet and Mesaba deposits – two large, distinct, and well-defined copper-nickel PGM resources in the Iron Range mining region of Minnesota. The NorthMet project is further along in the development process than the Mesaba project.
Litigation: Evidence of Litigation: Environmental groups have not been successful in combining Mesaba in the same lawsuits involving NorthMet.
Reasons for Concern: Water Quality: Water quality concerns are based on the project’s location straddling the boundary of the Rainy River and Lake Superior watersheds. Rain and snow falling on the north side of the divide flows into the Rainy River basin, which includes the Boundary Waters; water on the other side ends up in the St. Louis River and eventually Lake Superior.
Reasons for Support: Tax Revenue: State and local tax revenue generation

Location: Additional Location Information: Located 90 miles east of Phoenix, near Miami (pop 1,532, 2023) and six miles west of the city of Globe (pop 7,249, 2020), Arizona. 
Project Description: Mining Method: The Project includes an open-pit copper mine, a smelter and a rod mill. Miami is no longer mining ore, but currently produces copper through leaching material already placed on stockpiles, which is expected to continue through at least 2025.   
Project Description: Status of Project: The developer, in a 2024 technical conference paper, reported on sustainability improvements at its Miami smelter operation.                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Commercial Plans: Processing Done by the Same Lead Developer/Parent Company: The Miami smelter processes copper concentrate primarily from the developer's Arizona copper mines. In addition, because sulphuric acid is a by-product of smelting concentrates, the Miami smelter is a significant source of sulphuric acid for the developer's North America leaching operations.

Location: Additional Location Information: Located in the Upper Peninsula of Michigan, within 1.7 miles of the high-grade Eagle Nickel Mine — the only active nickel mine in the USA today — and only 0.4 miles from the Humboldt Mill (processing); The mine is located in Western Marquette County, Upper Peninsula, Michigan; closest town, 15 miles away, is Big Bay (pop 257, 2020); Marquette (pop 20,629, 2020) is 33 miles away. 
Project Description: Existing Mine: New drilling, but two miles from current Eagle mine in Michigan
Project Description: Status of Project: The develper sought a lease from the Michigan Department of Natural Resources (DNR) to drill on more than 23,000 public acres in Baraga, Houghton, Iron and Marquette counties.  MDNR granted the lease in 2024. In October 2024 the developer announced discovery of new nickel-copper reserves at Boulderdash target.  
Developer Description: Parent Company: UPX is subsidiary of Sweetwater Royalties, see Note on change in ownership. 
Developer Description: Was There Change in Ownership during Project?: Talon has entered into an option agreement with UPX to acquire up to an 80% ownership interest in the Michigan nickel properties. Under the agreement terms, Talon has agreed to a minimum spending obligation of up to $5 million in exploration expenditures or drilling of at least 7,500 meters.
Commercial Plans: Processing Plan in US: Nearby in Mercer County, North Dakota.  
Financial Support: Federal Agency: In September 2023, the Department of Defense awarded Talon $20.6 million in grant funding from the Defense Production Act to explore and discover more high-grade nickel mineralization in Michigan and Minnesota. The Department of Defense also agreed to provide a grant of $20.4 million to help support exploration and the feasibility study.  In 2022 the U.S. Department of Energy awarded Talon $114 million to develop a nickel ore processing plant in Mercer County, North Dakota.
Land Ownership: Type of Land:The developer acquired rights to explore for nickel on 400,000 private acres in the Upper Peninsula.  The developer has also requested a lease to drill on nearby public land. Michigan Department of Natural Resources granted 23,000 acres of mineral leases.

Location: Additional Location Information: Located north of the Mexican border, 10 miles from Sahuarita (35,638, 2022), 15 miles south of Tucson, Arizona; adjacent to the Twin Buttes mine and the Sierrita Mine. The mine is named for the nearby Mission San Xavier del Bac, an impressive and historic Franciscan mission dating back to the late 17th century.
Location: Mining District: Comprised of the Mission, Eisenhower, Pima, Mineral Hill and South San Xavier properties, as well as the neighboring North San Xavier mine.         
Project Description: Status of Project: In 2024 the developer commissioned an analysis of options for a new tailings disposal area.  
Commercial Plans: Processing Done by the Same Lead Developer/Parent Company: The Mission complex comprises open pit mining of the Mission, Eisenhower, Pima, Mineral Hill, North San Xavier and South San Xavier properties. The complex also includes two concentrator facilities, the Mission Mill (also known as the North Mill) and the South Mill. Underground mining stopped in 2003. The South mill was placed on ‘care and maintenance' in 2002 and re-opened in 2007. Control of dust emissions is a key operating priority with residential build up close to the mine-site.
Litigation: Evidence of Litigation: The developer and its unions have experienced a protracted labor dispute for several years. In 2024 the National Labor Relations Board was still prosecuting its 2022 case of unfair labor practices against Asarco in an ongoing trial before an administrative law judge in Phoenix. The unions also are pursuing more recent NLRB charges over Asarco’s allegedly unlawful withdrawal of union recognition at the Mission Mine in Sahuarita and the Silver Bell Mine near Marana. The NLRB has declined the unions’ request to hear those allegations as part of the larger pending case, but the agency has issued a complaint on those charges and plans to investigate and hear them separately. 
Concerned Interest Groups: Indigenous Groups: Currently, there is only one active copper mine on designated tribal lands in Arizona, the Mission Mine.

Project Name: Project also called Libby Exploration Project
Location: Additional Location Information: Located 23 miles south of Libby (pop 2,775, 2020), the county seat of Lincoln County, in northwestern Montana; Libby is at the confluence of Libby Creek and the Kootenai River.
Project Description: Existing Mine: Noranda Minerals initiated development of the Libby Exploration Project in 1989 but halted it in 2001, maintaining only reclamation work. In 2015, Hecla Mining acquired the project, along with the Montanore and Rock Creek mines in Montana. In 2022, Hecla decided to focus on obtaining new permits for the Montanore mine, putting the Rock Creek mine on the backburner.
Project Description: Status of Project: A new Plan of Operations for the Libby Exploration project limited to underground exploration and evaluation activities was submitted to the U.S. Forest Service and is currently under an Environmental Assessment review. The developer is making another effort (November 2024) to replace the old water permit with a new water permit.  If it is approved, the new permit would take the place of the active permit issued in 2006, which Montana DEQ proposes to terminate. DEQ previously issued a renewal permit in 2017, which was vacated by the Montana Supreme Court in 2020 following litigation. The new permit reassesses and updates how the developer will meet applicable water quality standards. 
Developer Description: Was There Change in Ownership during Project?: Hecla acquired the Libby Exploration (Montanore) Project in September 2016 with the acquisition of Mines Management Inc. 
Commercial Plans: Planned Production Capacity: A 2011 PEA stated the mine would produce 58,873,000 tons at 1.9oz/st silver and 0.7% copper.
Land Ownership: Type of Land: Cabinet Mountains Wilderness
Statements of Support from Public Officials: Local: In Libby, just 18 miles from Montanore’s development adit, signs declaring “We Support Montanore” are common in storefront windows.                                        
Statements of Support from Public Officials: State: Gov. Greg Gianforte has spoken favorably of the proposed mines in the past, and in 2020 he held a campaign event at Hecla’s offices in Libby. During that event, he criticized state and federal officials for how long it has taken to permit the two mines.
Litigation: Evidence of Litigation: Since Hecla’s acquisition, the project has faced numerous legal challenges. One lawsuit concerned the validity of the developer’s water discharge permit; the other suit alleged that the developer should not be allowed to proceed on the project because the CEO was covered by the state’s “bad actor” law due to the company’s bankruptcy and behaviors in the 1990s that caused unremediated contamination at the site.  A coalition of tribes and environmental groups initiated both lawsuits.  The second lawsuit became moot when the CEO stepped down in early 2024.
Litigation: Level of Court: Affirming the district court, the Montana Supreme Court in November 2020 invalidated the water permit that the state had awarded the developer many years earlier.  The developer was required to request a new water permit, if it wished to proceed. 
Concerned Interest Groups: Indigenous Groups: Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes, Fort Belknap Indian Community, Ksanka Elders Advisory Committee.
Concerned Interest Groups: Scale of Environmental Groups: National -- Earthjustice, Earthworks; Local/Regional -- Earthworks, Montana Environmental Information Center, Clark Fork Coalition, Rock Creek Alliance, Montana Conservation Voters, Save Our Cabinets, Cabinet Resources Group.
Concerned Interest Groups: Recreational Groups: Montana Trout Unlimited.
Reasons for Concern: Site of Historical, Cultural, Spiritual Significance: Coalition of Tribal groups and environmental groups view Montanore project as a threat to the sacred and pristine Cabinet Mountains Wilderness.
Reasons for Concern: Impact on Species: The Coalition against the mine is working to protect some of Montana’s most iconic species in the Cabinet Mountains, including grizzly bears, wolverines, and bull trout.  Grizzly bears and bull trout are both listed as threatened species under the federal Endangered Species Act. 
Reasons for Concern: Reputation of the Developer/Parent Company: In 2018, Hecla's CEO was labeled a “bad actor” under Montana law due to his past association with Pegasus, leading to prolonged litigation.

Location: Additional Location Information: Located 11 miles northeast of Greenville (pop 1,026, 2022, 75% of buildings destroyed in 2021 fire) in northeastern California near the Nevada line (100 miles northwest of Reno, Nevada).  
Project Description: Mining Method: open-pit. 
Project Description: Existing Mine: Historical production of 161 million pounds of copper at 2.2% grade from 1915 to 1930; Placer-Amex owned site from 1962-1994.
Project Description: Status of Project: Developer is now preparing to initiate an expansion drill program to include the higher-grade Superior and/or Engels deposits near the Moonlight deposit; initial version of PEA completed in 2018 under prior owner covered only Moonlight deposit. 
Project Description: Regulatory Challenges: Vesting Rights Issue -- Developer has requested vesting rights from the Plumas County Planning Department, which would allow developer to proceed with some permits and without an extensive California Environmental Quality Act analysis (request has led to community debates in associated public comment period).  Even if vesting is granted, a reclamation plan and adequate financial assurance for new mining must be approved by the County with input from the State.  The Plumas County Board of Supervisors adopted its first zoning ordinance on July 8, 1958, which has been identified as the date of vesting in the US Copper filing. Engels has been host to a range of different mining and forest activities over the years, before and after 1958.  In April 2024 the developer withdrew its request for vesting rights after County legal consultants concluded the case was not firmly established. The developer must strengthen the case or go through normal County permit procedures and California Environmental Quality Analysis.
Developer Description: Lead Developer: US Copper Corporation (Canada), since 2013 (previously several junior Canadian firms).
Commercial Plans: Planned Production Capacity: 150,000 tons of copper concentrate per year (Moonlight only).  
Commercial Plans: Planned Lifespan of Mine: 17 years (Moonlight only).
Developer Description: Was There Change in Ownership during Project?: Yes -- Placer-Amex was previous owner 
Commercial Plans: Processing Done by the Same Lead Developer/Parent Company: on-site facility.
Land Ownership: Type of Land: Private (owned by California-Engles Mining Company which has leased the land for mining for several decades).  Developer acquired 132 unpatented claims and a lease for the 36 patents covering the Superior and Engels mines.  Developer controls 13 square miles of land.  Might eventually require use of adjacent Forest Service land.  
Concerned Interest Groups: Community Residents/Groups: Filed comments against developer’s request for vesting rights; Citizen concerns expressed at public meetings -- increased traffic, tap on limited freshwater supplies, water contamination with toxics, disrupt beauty of rural community 
Concerned Interest Groups: Scale of Environmental Groups: Local -- Feather River Watershed Alliance

Location: Additional Location Information: Located 50 miles north of Safford (pop 10,271, 2020) in southeast Arizona.  
Project Description: Existing Mine: Operational since the 1880s
Project Description: Status of Project: The Morenci mine is by far the #1 copper-producing mine in the U.S. According to one tally, it is the 7th largest copper-producing mine in the world; In June 2024 the CEO of Morenci stated her intention to aggressively increase production due to the heightened global demand for copper.  
Developer Description: Lead Developer: Freeport McMoRan (72%) has majority- Sumitomo (15%), SMM Morenci (13%).
Commercial Plans: Processing Done by the Same Lead Developer/Parent Company: Processing on site, with plans to increase from 90,000 tonnes to 130,000 tonnes by 2024-2036.
Financial Support: Federal Agency:In March 2024 Freeport-McMoRan was selected to receive $80 million through a cooperative agreement with the U.S. Department of Energy for a project to use geothermal energy to heat leaching stockpiles in Morenci and Safford and integrate battery energy storage and microgrid operations to improve electrical reliability in Morenci. By using geothermal energy, the project aims to generate clean, industrial-scale heat to enable the recovery over time of billions of pounds of residual copper through the company’s Leach to the Last Drop initiative from already mined material previously considered unrecoverable. The project could increase copper recovery by 25 million pounds or more annually, depending on the geothermal resources.
Concerned Interest Groups: Indigenous Groups: San Carlos Apache Tribe

Location: Additional Location Information: Located in the Mojave Desert in southeastern California. Accessed through the Bailey Road exit from the Interstate 15; 9 miles from Nevada line and 60 miles southwest of Las Vegas and 30 miles from Baker (pop 442, 2020), California. 
Project Description: Status of Project: The developer is implementing an expansion plan at Mountain Pass that led to a record level of output in early 2024. 
Developer Description: Lead Developer: The developer, which held unsuccessful merger talks this year with rival Lynas Rare Earths, has struggled in recent months (2024) with falling prices and stiff competition from Chinese rivals.
Developer Description: Was There Change in Ownership during Project?: Mine purchased in 2017 from Molycorp, who in turn purchased the mine in 2007 from Chevron Corp.
Commercial Plans: Planned Production Capacity: 15% of global demand, 38,500mt of rare earths in concentrate.
Commercial Plans: Processing Plan in US: On site. Cost savings, as become only combined mine-processing facility in North America. China dominates global processing. MP Materials is investing $700 million to develop rare-earth processing capabilities in the U.S., including separating NdPr oxide at Mountain Pass and establishing a facility in Fort Worth, Texas to produce alloys and magnets for EVs; aiming to produce finished magnets by 2025.
Financial Support: Federal Agency: $10 Million in 2020 to reopen after bankruptcy, later $35 million for processing facility on site. $58.5 million tax-credit allocation for construction of manufacturing facility. Section 48C Advanced Energy Project. The most recent award went to Lynas Corp for a new commercial-scale heavy rare-earth oxide production facility on the Gulf coast of Texas; Mountain Pass was seen as a possible supplier of some mined material.  
Financial Support: Public Supply Agreement w/ an Automaker or Battery/Component Producer: GM deal 2021, long term customer.
Statements of Support from Public Officials: Federal: Biden Administration expressed support for mine in connection with signing of Executive Order 14017.
Statements of Concern from Public Officials: Local: County filed suit over pollution concerns in 2002, difficult relationship with new developer but relationship has improved.
Reasons for Support: Historical Mining or Reclamation Issues: Mismanagement of tailings causing air and water pollution under previous owner (Chevron), who paid more than $1.4 million in fines and settlements in county lawsuit; mine then closed until 2004.

Location: Additional Location Information: Located 30 miles from village of Paxson (pop 26, 2020), 50 miles south of the City of Delta Junction (pop 958, 2010) on the southern flank of Alaska Range, 125 miles southeast of Fairbanks, Southeast Fairbanks Census area, Alaska. 
Project Description: Status of Project: Exploration. The Nikolai Project is comprised of two blocks of claims – Eureka and Canwell – that each host compelling nickel targets.  The developer’s 2023 drilling program explored Eureka while the 2024 program explored Canwell, which is 13 miles northeast of Eureka.  Both programs uncovered massive deposits of nickel, copper, and cobalt.  
Developer Description: Lead Developer: Alaska Energy Metals Corporation (AEMC), USA (100% owner), company renamed early 2013, previously Millrock Resources Inc.
Developer Description: Was There Change in Ownership during Project?: Nico sold to Vale in the 1990s, which sold to junior miner Pure Nickel Inc (extensive drilling from 2007-2014), which sold data and rights to Millrock Resources, later renamed AEMC. 
Land Ownership: Type of Land: The Eureka claim block consists of 104 State of Alaska mining claims (6734 hectares) and is 100% owned by the developer.  The Canwell claim block consists of 42 State of Alaska mining claims (2720 hectares), with an option to purchase 100% interest in the claims from the underlying owner. In total, the project covers 94.54 km2 (9454 hectares).

Location: Additional Location Information: 9 miles north of the village of Carvers; 45 miles north of town of  Tonopah (pop 2,478, 2010); Big Smoky Valley, Nye County, Nevada, 143 miles east of Reno                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Project Description: Mining Method:  Lithium clays and brine exploration.                                                                                                                                                                                      
Project Description: Status of Project: 2023-2024 included electromagnetic sounding and soil sampling and drilling in the Carvers area; followed by electromagnetic sounding in the Austin area.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           Developer Description: Lead Developer: Morella Corporation (Australia) has a 60% earn-in interest through cash, stock and exploration and development progress.                                               Land Ownership: Type of Land: 3,400 acres (1,375 hectares); Claims divided into Carvers and Austin areas.

Location: Additional Location Information: Located in northeast Minnesota, about six miles south of Babbitt (pop 1,397, 2020) and one mile south of the existing Northshore iron-ore mine. Processing of mined ore would take place at the former LTV taconite plant near Hoyt Lakes (pop 2,020, 2020). Situated within the Partridge River intrusion along the northern margin of Duluth Complex, a geological formation near the Mesabi Iron Range.
Project Description: Status of Project: Minnesota Department of Natural Resources delayed permit decision until August 2025; Developer is working on new studies to enhance the sustainability of the project.
Project Description: Regulatory Challenges: The Army Corps of Engineers – with support from Biden EPA – revoked a critical federal water-quality permit due to concerns that waste from mine construction might endanger the water quality of a nearby tribal community.
Developer Description: Was There Change in Ownership during Project?: Project formerly called PolyMet. The ownership has been changed to a 50-50 joint venture of Polymet Mining (USA) and Teck Resources (Canada). The joint venture controls both the NewRange Copper Nickel deposit and Teck’s Mesaba deposit a few miles to the east.; In February 2023 the Swiss multinational Glencore became a 100% owner of the Polymet side of the joint venture.; Teck’s largest shareholder is the China Investment Corp., the sovereign wealth fund of the Beijing government, with a 10% stake.
Land Ownership: Public Land Ownership: USFS Superior National Forest Service
Litigation: Evidence of Litigation: After the developer obtained all necessary permits for the project,  a coalition of environmental and tribal groups initiated numerous lawsuits at different times and in different venues.  Those lawsuits challenged the validity of the land swap that allowed the developer to acquire crucial land for the project, the general permit to construct and operate the mine, the water quality permit, the air permit, and the dam safety permit related to waste management at the mine.  The plaintiffs had the most success with their challenges to the general permit to operate and construct the mine and their challenges to the water quality permit.  Both permits were ultimately overturned by the Minnesota Supreme Court.
Concerned Interest Groups: Indigenous Groups: Fond du Lac Band of Lake Superior Chippewa
Concerned Interest Groups: Scale of Environmental Groups: Local/Regional -- WaterLegacy, Conservation Minnesota, Friends of the Boundary Waters Wilderness and the Minnesota Center for Environmental Advocacy
Supportive Interest Groups: Commercial Groups: MiningMinesota

Location: Additional Location Information: Located immediately west of Death Valley National Park in California near the Nevada border; nearest towns are Pahrump (pop 44,738, 2020), Nevada, Searles Valley (pop 1,565, 2020), California, and Darwin (pop 26, 2020), California.
Project Description: Status of Project: Since at least 2019 indigenous groups and environmentalists have clashed with the developer over requests that BLM allow exploratory drilling at Panamint Valley.  In February 2024 the developer again submitted to BLM a plan of operations, a necessary step toward approval of an exploratory drilling program; despite some opposition, BLM approved the proposal in August 2024.  
Developer Description: Parent Company: Founded in 2010; current project portfolio includes copper, gold, and lithium assets in the US, Kazakhstan, and Mongolia 
Concerned Interest Groups: Indigenous Groups: Friends of the  Inyo
Concerned Interest Groups: Scale of Environmental Groups: National -- Sierra Club, Defenders of Wildlife, Center for Biological Diversity; Local/Regional -- Basin and Range Watch, Great Basin Water Network
Reasons for Concern: Impacts to Natural Environment: Neighbors Death Valley National Park 
Reasons for Concern: Water Quality: Environmental groups allege that the environmental assessment does not include mapping of floodplain boundaries, nor any hydrologic modeling or analysis.  They also contend there could be cross contamination from the deep brines to the freshwater aquifer.  Further, they argue the drill site reclamation practices are inadequate to protect water.  
Reasons for Concern: Impact on Species: Sanctuary for desert bighorn sheep; sanctuary for the Inyo California Towhee (threatened species); desert tortoise; Panamint alligator lizard.
Reasons for Concern: Recreation: Neighbors Death Valley National Park

Location: Additional Location Information:  Located 19 miles west of the town of Salmon (pop 3,295, 2023), central Idaho; 2 miles east of Jervois’ Idaho Cobalt Operation.
Location: Mining District: Blackbird District (2 miles to the northeast of the historic Blackbird Cobalt Mine).
Project Description: Existing Mine: Has undergone small-scale past production at the historic Sweet Repose Mine.
Project Description: Status of Project: Koba is planning additional geochemical sampling, mapping and geophysical surveying to help delineate targets for drilling.; The project was actively explored between 2017 and 2018, when ePower Metals Inc (now Prime Mining Corp) collected a total of 1,534 soils samples, 53 surface rock samples and 29 underground samples; Koba Resources reports in its FY 2024 Annual Report that no significant work was done at its cobalt projects in FY 2024.
Developer Description: Lead Developer: Koba Resources Limited acquired the site in November of 2021. 
Developer Description: Was There Change in Ownership during Project?: Koba Resources was created when New World Resources (ASX: NWC) decided to spin-out its cobalt-copper assets.
Land Ownership: Type of Land: 870 hectare of public land; part of Salmon National Forest (USFS).

Location: Additional Location Information: Located in Paradox Basin (asymmetric foreland basin located mostly in southeast Utah and southwest Colorado), near Green River (pop 847, 2020) in southern Utah.
Project Description: Status of Project: In 2024 the developer’s request that the State of Utah approve its plan for exploration ran into concerns from an unusually diverse array of players: a coalition of environmental groups, local nonprofits, some local government agencies, and three federal agencies: the Bureau of Land Management, the National Park Service, and the Bureau of Reclamation.  The state approved the developer’s plan.  
Project Description: Regulatory Challenges: Federal agencies have raised concerns about the developer's plans to access groundwater near the Green River, which connects to the Colorado River.  Utah regulators will make the final decisions about water permits. Update: in June of 2024, Utah state officials suspended a key water permit for the Paradox Lithium project following concerns from conservation advocates about potential contamination and water overuse in the Green River. September 2024: the state doubled down on its original decision to approve, while requiring that the developer demonstrate that the process is truly non-consumptive; developer will be subject to fines if water is consumed. 
Developer Description: Lead Developer: In June 2024 the developer announced collaboration with Koch Technology Solutions (KTS), a Koch Engineered Solutions (KES) company, for the commissioning of its Li-Pro™ process pilot unit for lithium extraction at the developer's Green River Lithium Project. The pilot will be jointly funded by the developer and an investment from KTS through a convertible note as the companies work to develop a further commercial relationship.
Commercial Plans: Processing Done by the Same Lead Developer/Parent Company: Potentially developing a processing plan onsite, now in engineering stages.
Financial Support: Public Supply Agreement w/ an Automaker or Battery/Component Producer: In 2024 the developer completed negotiations with LG Energy Solution and executed its first binding offtake term sheet to supply battery-grade lithium carbonate. The agreement calls for the developer to supply up to 4,000 dry metric tonnes per year of battery-grade lithium carbonate. The associated volumes represent approximately 40 percent of the Project’s start-up production capacity of 10,000 tonnes per year.
Statements of Support from Public Officials: State: Sen. Nate Blouin, D-Salt Lake City and Sen. Scott Sandall, R-Tremonton
Statements of Concern from Public Officials: Local: Town of Green River residents concerned about water usage
Statements of Concern from Public Officials: Federal: Bureau of Land Management raised concerns about the developer's plans to pump 13,755 acre-feet per year of groundwater near the Green River. Department officials said the aquifer and the river were connected and the developer had not sufficiently explained how the groundwater withdrawals might affect the Green River. National Park Service also filed a letter of concern.
Litigation: Evidence of Litigation: In October 2024, a coalition of conservationists, businesses, and residents sued the Utah Division of Water Rights in the State’s 7th District Court in Moab to overturn the Division’s decision to approve water rights for lithium extraction.  The leader of the lawsuit is Great Basin Water Network.  The litigation was not resolved as of December 2024.
Concerned Interest Groups: Scale of Environmental Groups: Local/Regional -- Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance, Living Rivers, Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance, Utah Rivers Council and the Great Basin Water Network.
Concerned Interest Groups: Recreational Groups: Holiday River Expeditions.
Reasons for Concern: Water Supply: Water rights are sensitive in Utah; also concern of possible pollution of Green River.
Reason for Concern: Other: DLE technology is untested.
Reasons for Support: Employment: The developer plans to employ 80-320 people in rural Utah.

Location: Additional Location Information: Located near Miramiguoa Park (pop 120, 2020) in southeast Missouri.
Project Description: Existing Mine: Mining rare earths is a new development.
Project Description: Status of Project: The Pea Ridge mine would be among the first in the US to produce relatively large amounts of dysprosium, a critical element in electric motors.  The developer will use membrane solvent extraction technology to separate rare earths in mined ore through a licensing arrangement with the federal government’s Oak Ridge National Laboratory, a unit of the Department of Energy.  
Project Description: Regulatory Challenges:The regulatory requirements for management of radioactive thorium at the site could affect the commercial viability of the site and have slowed development. 
Commercial Plans: Processing Done by the Same Lead Developer/Parent Company: Caldera Holding has licensed ORNL's membrane solvent extraction technique to separate rare earth elements in mined ore. 
Reasons for Concern: Historical Mining or Reclamation Issues: Clean Water Act violations on site of previous mine, management of thorium, a radioactive element used to make nuclear fuel.

Location: County: Lake and Peninsula Borough.
Location: Additional Location Information: 200 miles southwest of Anchorage, near headwaters of the Bristol Bay, 17 miles northwest of the village of Iliamna (pop 108, 2020), Lake and Peninsula Borough, southwest Alaska
Project Description: Existing Mine: Deposits discovered in 1987 by Cominco Alaska (Teck Resources Ltd.), optioned by Northern Dynasty Minerals in 2001, explored in 2002, and drilled from 2002-2013 with discovery of Pebble East in 2005. Preparation for the permitting process began and administrative review lasted over 13 years.  
Project Description: Status of Project: Advanced exploration, but delayed indefinitely
Project Description: Regulatory Challenges: The developer has received multiple permits from the State for exploratory activities that have extended over a decade. In July 2020, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers published a final environmental impact statement (EIS) recommending development of the Pebble project. However, the federal government reversed its position at the urging of advisors to President Trump.  Later in 2020 the Trump Army Corps of Engineers rejected a permit application regarding disposal of dredge material that was critical for project development. On January 31, 2023, the EPA under Biden (who had made a campaign pledge to stop the mine) effectively vetoed the project, using a rarely invoked power under Section 404 (c) of the Clean Water Act to restrict development to protect watersheds. The EPA action, which bans the disposal of mine waste in part of the Bay’s watershed, safeguards a much larger area than what the developer had proposed to mine. This is the 14th time in the history of the Clean Water Act and just the third time in the past 30 years that EPA has used this veto authority.The developer appealed the Army Corp decision, arguing that the decision was inconsistent with the EIA (which the Corps had led with multiple federal, state and local agencies) but the Corps refused to act on the appeal, citing EPA’s decision to put the land off limits to mining. Separately, the Conservation Fund, an environmental preservation organization, purchased conservation easements for 44,000 acres of land owned by a Native village corporation near Iliamna Lake, about 20 miles south of the proposed mine site and the area covered by the E.P.A. ruling. The easements effectively block development and would make construction of an access road more difficult.  
Commercial Plans: Planned Production Capacity: 320 million lb copper; 368,000 oz gold; 15 million lb molybdenum; 1.8 million oz silver and 10,000 kg rhenium. 
Commercial Plans: Planned Lifespan of Mine: Mine's lifespan could be extended up to 100 years with mine expansions.
Commercial Plans: Processing Done by the Same Lead Developer/Parent Company: The open pit mine will feed a 180,000 copper flotation concentrator capable of processing 1.3 billion tons of mineralized material over 20 years of mining.  The PEA includes some expansion scenarios with a larger processing operation. 
Land Ownership: Type of Land: The developer holds mineral rights for 186 square miles (480 km2) of the area, an area that includes the Pebble deposits, as well as other, less explored, mineral deposits. 
Statements of Support from Public Officials: State: Gov. Mike Dunleavy said in a written statement that the EPA’s decision threatens the state’s legal right to develop its mineral resources, at a deposit that could be worth up to $1 trillion
Statements of Concern from Public Officials: Federal: Alaska's U.S. Senators Dan Sullivan and Lisa Murkowski, both Republicans, came out against the mine, saying it could cause significant damage to the Bristol Bay region, which is popular for fishing and hunting; Senator Maria Cantwell, Democrat of Washington, one of the first lawmakers to oppose the project, said she was “ecstatic” about the E.P.A. action. Washington State residents hold about a quarter of the commercial permits to fish for Bristol Bay sockeye, and much of the harvest passes through the state’s ports.
Litigation: Evidence of Litigation: Developer and State of Alaska sued the Army Corps of Engineers in the US District Court for the District of Alaska.seeking to override the permit denial. A separate lawsuit against EPA was filed by Iliamna Natives Limited and the Alaska Peninsula Corporation, alleging the EPA overstepped its authority with its final decision to block the Pebble Mine project; The State of Alaska has also sued the federal government seeking more than $700 billion in compensation in the US Court of Federal Claims in the District of Columbia. This is based on a 100-year estimate of what the mine would have done for economic development in Alaska; The developer has sued separately in the Federal Claims Court, citing that it has expended more than $1 billion acquiring the land and developing the site; the US Supreme Court in January 2024 declined to take up Alaska v United States, an emergency request from the State of Alaska to review the Biden EPA veto of the proposed Pebble copper and gold mine in the Bristol Bay watershed.  The Court’s decision forces Alaska to go through the lower federal courts with its concerns; the case could eventually make it to the Supreme Court for a merits ruling. 
Concerned Interest Groups: Indigenous Groups: Bristol Bay Native Corp., the region’s Alaska Native corporation and a mine opponent; United Tribes of Bristol Bay.
Concerned Interest Groups: Scale of Environmental Groups: National -- Echoing the concerns of environmental groups, EPA said that the mine’s harm to salmon habitat would be “unacceptable.” It said it would damage or destroy 100 miles of streams that support spawning and breeding and approximately 2,100 acres of surrounding wetlands
Concerned Interest Groups: Recreational Groups: Save Bristol Bay, organized by Trout Unlimited.
Concerned Interest Groups: Evidence of Organized Protest: Opponents protested in Anchorage, Alaska in 2019. 
Reasons for Concern: Site of Historical, Cultural, Spiritual Significance: Concern there could be harm to two dozen Native villages in the region.
Reasons for Concern: Impact on Species: Concern there could be harm to the world’s largest commercial sockeye salmon fishery.
Supportive Interest Groups: Commercial Groups: The lawsuit against EPA is filed by the Pacific Legal Foundation, a conservative public interest law practice that has fought for private property rights since it began in 1973.  Seeking to restrain EPA overreach and filing supportive briefs, too, were the Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority and numerous Alaska and national resource-development groups.
Reasons for Support: Economic Growth: Supported by some Alaskan lawmakers and Native groups for the economic benefits it would bring.

Location: Additional Location Information: Located 10 miles north of Patten (pop 771, 2020), east of Baxter State Park, northern Maine.
Project Description: Status of Project: The developer tried twice to persuade the Maine Land Use Planning Commission to modify zoning law to allow the project.  After the second try, the Commission voted, in 2023, 5 to 2 against a zoning change.
Project Description: Regulatory Challenges: Maine recently passed legislation that made securing the necessary permits for mining operations more intensive. The developer also faced zoning challenges that ultimately led to the proposed mine being delayed indefinitely; In 2023 the planning commission voted 5-2 against the rezoning petition from the developer. 
Developer Description: Was There Change in Ownership during Project?: Land previously owned by Getty Oil & Chevron who let the mineral leases for the property expire in 1998; acquired by current owner in 2017
Land Ownership: Type of Land: Leased land.  6781 acres was acquired by Wolfden Resources in 2017 for $8.5 million.
Statements of Support from Public Officials: Local: Town of Patten supports the project for increased development and population.
Statements of Support from Public Officials: State: State Sen. Trey Stewart supports for economic development
Concerned Interest Groups: Scale of Environmental Groups: Local/Regional -- Natural Resources Council of Maine; National -- National Parks Conservation Association, Earthjustice, Conservation Law Foundation
Reasons for Concern: Impacts to Natural Environment: Might adversel impact nearby national park.
Reasons for Concern: Site of Historical, Cultural, Spiritual Significance: Project might disrupt sacred sites near Mattawamkeag River, which is sacred to the Penobscot Nation. 
Reasons for Concern: Water Quality: Fears of toxic byproducts and acid mine drainage. 
Reasons for Concern: Classification of Species Impacted: Endangered atlantic salmon.
Reasons for Concern: Reputation of the Developer/Parent Company: The developer may lack the capabilities and financial resources to mine competently.
Reasons for Concern: Other: Impact on Tourism

Location: Additional Location Information: Located 8 miles west of the town of Miami (pop 1,532, 2023) in central Arizona; 80 miles east of Phoenix via Highway 60. 
Project Description: Status of Project: Active, In November 2021 the developer received final approvals from the US Forest Service for a new mine plan of operations, approved by the Tonto National Forest, extending Pinto Valley’s life to the year 2039.
Project Description: Regulatory Challenges: The 2021 decision of the USFS to expand the mine is the subject of a lawsuit by Earthjustice and other environmental groups against the USFS.
Developer Description: Was There Change in Ownership during Project?: Capstone acquired mine from BHP in October 2013. Capstone operates mine through affiliate Pinto Valley Mining.
Litigation: Evidence of Litigation: In September 2024, conservation groups sued the U.S. Forest Service and U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service for violating the National Environmental Policy Act, Endangered Species Act, and other laws in approving expanded operations at the Pinto Valley Mine, east of Phoenix. The litigation was not resolved as of December 2024.                                                                                       
Reasons for Concern: Impacts to Natural Environment: Pinto Valley’s operations overlap with parts of the Tonto National Forest. Pinto Valley’s plan to upgrade its TSF requires extension onto some land within the Tonto National Forest. 
Concerned Interest Groups: Environmental Groups EarthJustice, Audubon Society, Western Action Mining Project, Sierra Club.
Reason for Concern: Water Quality: Releases of Toxic Substances.  According to EPA data, the Pinto Valley Mine is the 4th largest source of toxic releases into the environment in the State of Arizona.    
Reason for Concern: Impact on Species: Consumption of scarce water supplies and possible damage to the habitat of threatened and endangered species, specifically the western yellow-billed cuckoo & southwestern willow flycatcher. In spite of this, the Forest Service and Fish and Wildlife Service did not require the developer to implement adequate mitigation measures that would protect water flows.
Reason for Concern: Classification of Species Impacted: Southwestern willow flycatcher (endangered); Western yellow-billed cuckoo (threatened).

Location: Additional Location Information: Located at the north end of the Lemhi Range, is near Baker (pop 68, 2020), central Idaho at the border with Montana; near entrance to Great Basin National Park; recent exploration work was 7 miles southeast of Salmon (3,295, 2023), Idaho.
